subtopic: EXTENSION OF AWARD OF CANADIAN GENERAL SERVICE BADGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief announcement in connection with the award of the Canadian general service badge. Up to the present, the award of this badge has been limited to men and women who served during the war in the armed forces of Canada. Provision was not made for the award of the badge to Canadians who served in the armed forces of Great Britain or any of the other dominions or other allied governments. In Great Britain no service badge was awarded and a number of Canadians who served in the British forces were not entitled to wear any badge. This applied particularly to a very large number of Canadians, about 4,000 in all who joined the Royal Air Force before and during the war. To meet these cases, it has been decided to extend the award of this badge to Canadians who served in the armed forces of any of the nations of the British commonwealth or allied countries.
Application by those who are entitled to the badge should be made to the director of records, Department of Veterans Affairs, No. 8 Temporary Building, Ottawa, who, after verifying eligibility, will transfer the applications to the Department of National Defence for issue of the badge.

speechtext:
1.	Has the governor in council or any minister the power to set an acreage for wheat production from which the wheat board will be authorized to accept deliveries of wheat regardless of what that delivery quota may be?
2.	If so, under what statute or order in council or regulation?
3.	How much wheat has been sold each week during the past six weeks to class I countries other than Great Britain, giving particulars of the countries and the amounts sold to each and the price per bushel in each case?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: WHEAT-DELIVERY QUOTA-SETTING OF ACREAGE FOR PRODUCTION
speechtext:
1.	The governor in council has not, nor has any minister, the power to control the production of wheat either by setting an acreage for production, or otherwise.
Under the Canadian Wheat Board Act, the Canadian wheat board is empowered to fix from time to time quotas of each kind of grain that may be delivered by producers to elevators or railway cars within any period or periods either generally or in specified areas, or at specified delivery points, or otherwise.
"Quota" is defined in the said act as "the quantity of grain authorized to be delivered from the grain produced on land described in the permit book as fixed from time to time by the board, whether expressed as a quantity that may be delivered from a specified number of acres, or otherwise."
2.	Answered by (1).
3.	If by class I countries are meant countries receiving wheat at the price of $1.55 per bushel, basis No. 1 Northern, in store Fort William Port Arthur, Vancouver or Churchill, the answer is that no country other than Great Britain receives wheat at this price.

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the fact that Newfoundland delegates have been here for some time, and that we are hoping this will be the last day of the session, I should like to ask the minister if he is in a position to give us a progress report with respect to the discussions as to the future relations of Newfoundland and Canada. I have not given the minister any notice of this question. I should be

satisfied to have him delay bis answer until later on in the day, but I think that before we leave some statement should be made.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): I do not think that I would be in any better position later in the day than I am at this moment to answer the question. There have been several meetings with the delegation from Newfoundland, and at the last general meeting of their delegation with our representatives several subcommittees were established to consider various aspects of the problems being explored.
All I can say is that on both sides there is evidence of the sincerest desire to get at all such facts as it would be important for the citizenst of the two countries to consider in drawing their conclusions as to whether at this time it is possible to find a basis of closer union that would be of mutual advantage to the two countries. There is the sincerest desire on both sides to smooth out all suggestions of what at first might appear to be difficulties standing in the way. The matter has not progressed to a stage where anything definite can be stated about it, but it is further advanced than it was when this delegation came here, and the advance has been in the right direction. There are still very cordial and hopeful efforts being made on all sides to arrive at something that would appeal to the citizens of both countries.

speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the third reading of Bill No. 18, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Yesterday when this bill was before the committee of the whole house the temperature of hon. members had risen to such a degree that it would have been difficult, I fear, to secure agreement on a proposition as simple as twice two makes four. Earlier in the day I had suggested that the name "Wright," which a county on the north shore of the Ottawa has borne for several generations, be restored to it in place of the name "Gatineau" bestowed upon it by this bill. In the course of my remarks I contended that the issue was not political and I understood the right hon. gentleman who leads the house 'to say that he considered it in the same light and that it was one on which hon. members might express their opinion without regard to political allegiance. Later my hon. friend the member for Wright (Mr. Raymond) took part in the debate and advanced some reasons for the change of name.
I hope >that the hon. member for Wright will not think that I am attempting in any way to dictate to the people of his constituency or even to suggest to them that they have not the complete right to express views concerning a matter which affects them primarily. On the other hand, I hope that the hon. gentleman will not consider me impertinent if I say to him that sometimes people do in haste things they would not do rMr. Fulton.]
had they considered them a little more maturely. There is a principle at stake, I believe, which probably most people would not be willing to abandon without some thought. The whole continent, on both sides of the international line, is studded with the names of great precursors, the names of men of daring, the names of men who went forth into the wilderness and planted there the seeds of Christianity, of civilization, of culture and industry. We owe it to the future to preserve these names.
The hon. member for Wright said some things about the Gatineau river and the souvenirs which it recalls, the hardihood of the many people who have laboured along its shores. That is well and good, and I share his generous sentiment to the fullest extent. But there was a man who was probably the first to fell trees on the shores of that majestic stream, and I am suggesting to my hon. friend that it is well that his name be not forgotten. The name Gatineau is well preserved. The stream itself is a mighty one and for a long time has been an important highway in the development of our north country. The provincial county of Gatineau is, after all, the official area on which municipal divisions are based and on which the whole municipal and educational fabric rests. Registration and other branches of our civil government rest on provincial county divisions. A federal electoral division is something superimposed on the civil divisions which are essentially provincial. To permit this electoral division to retain the name of that great man who, after all, was the father of what has become the national capital-it was Wright who established the settlement which later extended to and became Ottawa-so that the name of Wright may be kept alive is something that I think we should all wish to do. There is fame and glory enough to go around. There is enough for everyone. I do not think we are adding to the interest of the story of Canada by eliminating a name like that of Wright.
I intend to move an amendment; I ask the house if it will not reconsider the somewhat heated and hurried decision reached yesterday. I am going to ask the hon. member for Wright if in all these circumstances he does not feel that he can support an amendment which would restore to that fine district in the Gatineau valley the name of Wright. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) that the word "Gatineau" which appears under item 18 in the Quebec schedule, be replaced by the name of "Wright", which was the name that area has borne for several generations.

However, I cannot let the opportunity pass without expressing my sympathy for the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Lacomfoe). He is an old colleague of mine and has been in the House of Commons for a great number of years. He was elected some time after I myself was elected, and he was reelected by his constituents at each election except one. Of course he has personal views. No one is bound to agree with all he has said in his various speeches. The membership of the house creates a close association between members of parliament. Personally I have disagreed with others at times, but not all the time, and I have received some support from my Liberal colleagues, from members of the Progressive Conservative group, from some C.C.F. members and some Social Credit members, and even from the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains. I find it pitiful that a constituency of such long-standing disappears from the map. I understand the feelings of the hon. gentleman, and I would perhaps have found stronger words in tihe dictionary than those he used if the same thing had been done to me.
I was speaking a moment ago about the close association which exists between all members of parliament. We are in the same boat. We have to make the best of it. Even when I disagree with any one of my colleagues, I am readly to give him credit for some quality which has been acknowledged by his constituents who have given him a majority in the previous election. Mr. Speaker, just before you leave the chair on this motion there is a word

or two I should like to say to the government, and particularly to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie). There are a few hours yet before this session will be over and it does seem to me that it is not too late for the government to do something for certain groups of people to whom no consideration has been given during this session. I shall not take the time to enumerate the various groups which I feel have been overlooked; there are a great many, but there are two that I wish to mention. I know that I have the support of all members of the house with respect to these two groups of people.
First of all, I refer to widows of non-pen-sioned veterans. At the moment the only provision for these widows made by the government is under the War Veterans Allowance Act, and the maximum payment is $30.41 per month. I know the kind of thing that can be said about raising a matter of this kind at this stage of the session, but I ask the government to face the fact that it simply is not fair to ask these women to get along on such a small amount of money. This applies also to the second group I have in mind, namely veterans who have to live on the so-called burnt-out pension, properly known as a war veterans allowance. In this case the maximum amount paid to a single veteran is the same figure of $30.41 per month.
When that figure was set I did not think it was sufficient, but one argument advanced in favour of it was that it was a little higher than the amount of the old age pension and similar benefits in effect at that time. The old age pension has now been raised to a basic amount of $30. per month and in some provinces it is more than that. In fact, this government is urging the provinces to add to the $30, to make it $40 or something more. It has been recognized that more than S30 per month is needed to live on, and I think it is most unfair to ask these veterans' widows and burnt-out pensioners to get along on $30.41 per month.
I know the sympathy to which I have referred is just as strong in the heart of the Minister of Veterans Affairs as it is in the hearts of the rest of us, but in addition to the sympathy he may have in his heart the minister has power in the position which he occupies. I am making an appeal to him and to his colleagues to find some way before this session closes to raise that amount. To allow these people only $30.41 a month is a disgrace.
I Shall not go into all the arguments we have brought forward on previous occasions during this session with regard to increases

Pensions and War Veterans Allowances
in the cost of living and the way we feel about the manner in which those increases have been permitted to occur. The fact is that the cost of living has gone up since that figure of $30.41 per month or $365 per year was set. I am sure that this matter appeals so definitely to the hearts and minds of hon. members that nothing more need be said All of us have had appeals made to us in recent months to do something for groups of people of this kind before the session ends. I am sure that I have the support of hon. members to my right and of hon. members to my left, and I know there is support among hon. members across the way. I hope hon. members from all quarters in the house will join me in asking the government to do something about this matter before this session ends.

Otherwise the session will last two weeks more. I have come here after spending the summer in a most delightful spot. I have come here at great sacrifice. I am here on parliamentary business and I want to be respected as a member of parliament. I do not want to witness another performance such as occurred last night at the closing of the house. That is not a threat, it is a warning. I want the acting leader of the house to be just as polite as the Prime Minister and the rest of his colleagues. I do not want him to bully anyone. I want him to realize that the position he holds is a position of honour and he must prove himself qualified for it. I have waited for a long time to say this.
I am scandalized that the estimates of veterans affairs are coming at the very last hour of the very last day. A great deal of money has been spent for veterans and it is time for us to know how it has been spent

Mr. Speaker, I wish to support the remarks made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Temiseouata (Mr. Pouliot). I think it is most unfortunate that the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs are to be practically the last, according to the statement which the minister has just made, to come before us. At this late hour it will be impossible to give the estimates of this most important department of government the careful consideration which they merit. There is no question, Mr. Speaker, that the Department of Veterans Affairs is to many, many hundreds of thousands of Canadians the most important department of government today, and I would suggest to the minister that even at this late hour he give most serious consideration to the recommendations made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that the War Veterans Allowance Act should be amended with a view to increasing the allowances to make them equal at least to the amount now paid to old age pensioners, and that consideration also be given to the non-pensioned widows, not only the widows of veterans who did not receive a pension but also the widows of veterans who received a pension up to the time of their death but whose disability pension was less than fifty per cent, thereby disentitling the widow to pension.
I point out to the minister that in my opinion it is most essential that we should have in this house a standing committee on veterans affairs. If we had such a committee

Pensions and War Veterans Allowances
functioning as the special war veterans committee has functioned in a very efficient manner in the last two sessions of parliament, thereby relieving the house of a great deal of tedious work, it could have reviewed the War Veterans Allowances Act to provide for these two classes of pensioners.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was not with regard to taking up the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs. It had to do with three other matters which we think are of importance at this time. First there was the question of the disability pension for the returned man from this war who is totally disabled and, if married, gets a pension of $100 a month for himself and his wife and $75 a month if he is single. Second, there are a number of widows of veterans of the last war whose pension is only $30.41 if they receive full pension, but many of whom, through some mistake on their part but more often mistakes made by some government department, do not receive the full pension. I know of one. case, the widow of a soldier of the first great war who had two sons fighting in the last war and who was receiving the war veterans allowance and the widow's pension, the two cheques being sent out at the same time. Today she is living on $27.41 a month, with a son who was severely wounded and lost an eye at Hong Kong and is unable to obtain suitable employment. He receives some $45 a month. He used to help support his mother both before going overseas and during the time he was overseas.
In view of the answers I have received from the government to date indicating that we are going to have an increased cost of living in this country this fall when the subsidies on grain are taken off and costs are increased to the producers in eastern Canada which will result in higher prices for agricultural products, and with the subsidy of 78 cents a bushel coming off wheat that is being milled for flour, which will mean an increase of three cents a loaf in the price of bread, there is no doubt in my mind and I am sure in the minds of the members of this house that the cost of living is going to increase this fall and1 winter, and I think we would be derelict in our duty if we left this house

Pensions and War Veterans Allowances
without indicating to the government that we believe something should be done with respect to this matter. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden):
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be left out, and the following words be inserted instead thereof:
This house is of the opinion that the government should give immediate consideration to the amending of the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act so as to provide increases in the basic disability pension, the war veterans' allowance, and the allowance to veterans' widows and orphans, to enable those receiving these pensions and allowances to meet the increased cost of living.

In seconding this motion I should like it to be noted by the house that we are not making any special reference to the ordinary people of Canada who are supporting this government in its policy of lifting controls. The cost of living is going up. Owing to the fact that the government have set its rate of pension at $75 for a single person who is totally disabled, and $100 for a married man and that the pensions for widows with children were set at a time when the cost of living was not as high as it is at this time, we are making a special appeal on behalf of veterans and veterans' dependents to meet the situation in which they find themselves, and which they are incapable of meeting themselves. We are talking about veterans who are totally disabled but whose pension has not been increased. Because the cost of living is constantly rising it puts them in a position where their standard of living is going down below that which we should allow as legislators of this country.
We are making a special appeal at this particular time that special legislation be brought in now to meet the situation. The house is not likely to meet again until next
February. These veterans are stuck. It is quite evident that controls are to be lifted and the cost of living is going up. Much can happen between now and when this house meets again and passes through the regular procedure which is necessary before any legislation can be brought in to increase these pensions. The matter should be dealt with. It is an emergency situation: Efforts should be taken to improve the lot of people who are going to suffer under the presently existing circumstances. We renew our plea that this house and the government in particular take this matter into serious consideration at this time in behalf of people who have done so much for Canada.

subtopic: PENSIONS AND WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCES- AMENDMENT-MR. WRICHT
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words in support of this amendment. I have no doubt that the government is not very happy about an amendment of this kind being brought in at this stage of the session, but it would not have happened had the estimates of veterans affairs been brought up for consideration at an earlier date. The attempt of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to switch the onus for that delay onto the opposition parties is ridiculous. At the end of each day's sittings, as the business of the house for the following day was announced, the Department of Veterans Affairs frequently was listed, but always mysteriously it has turned out that the Department of Veterans Affairs is at the end, and the government must take full responsibility for that fact.
Hon. members will realize that in the 1945 and 1946 sessions we had a special committee on veterans affairs where all these problems could be thoroughly discussed. This year there has been no opportunity whatever from the beginning of the session until today to have a discussion on veterans affairs. After all the obstacles possible had been put in our way we did manage to bring about a discussion on the unfairness to merchant seamen, but there has been no chance to have a proper debate on veterans affairs.
The position is this. Old age pensions have been increased. This government has announced as its policy that it is not setting the proper rate for old age pension required for the maintenance of a person without any other income, but is simply making a maintenance grant, paying three-quarters of what they call a maintenance grant; in other words, three-quarters of $30. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has admitted several times that $30 is not enough for a person to live on; that it if only meant to be
5736	COMMONS
Pensions and War Veterans Allowances
a maintenance grant and that it is the responsibility of the provinces to pay whatever additional amount is required to enable our senior citizens to live. The veterans are the direct responsibility of this dominion parliament; they are not the responsibility of the provinces. Last Saturday the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) said that in so far as housing is concerned he accepted responsibility for the veterans, but for nobody else, and the government cannot get away from the fact that the responsibility for the veterans of Canada rests right here in the House of Commons. The veteran is able to get only $30.41 as a war veterans allowance. That is admittedly not a large enough sum for him to live on. The onus for increasing that to a living amount rests on the dominion government. That is one of the main reasons why this amendment is so important.
During the discussion on old age pensions I pointed out this fact to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and he said that there would be a committee next year at which time the whole question could be considered. That means a delay of a year with nothing being done to help these veterans who receive war veterans allowances, and delay of a year is a very serious thing to men of that age.
The position with regard to pensioners is also serious, particularly the widows and the children whose father was lost in the war. There must be some change made, and made quickly, to benefit them. I suggest to the government that the time has now come to make provision that the children of the soldier who lost his life in the war shall get the same educational benefits as the father would have received had he returned to Canada. There are different other questions which I will not go into any further at this stage, but I do say that this amendment is timely, and that these problems should have been faced by the government many weeks ago.

That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be left out, and the following words be inserted therefor.

If the amendment were to carry it would be in the nature of a want of confidence motion in the government and the government will have to resign, and there would then be no opportunity for any government immediately to consider the condition and wellbeing of the veterans, their widows and orphans. That is the position. As I say, it is all right to bring up the question at this time to be discussed; I welcome that in the fullest possible way but I want hon. members to understand the significance of the motion as it is worded and which if carried would make it impossible for this government to consider any further at this time the question of the well-being of veterans and members of their families.

speechtext: Take the whips off and it will be all right.

My hon. friend perhaps knows more about parliamentary government than anyone, but may I say to him, whether the whips were off or not the effect would be exactly what I have described, and if he knew a little more about parliamentary procedure and practice he would have realized that.
I am making it quite clear that the government welcomes any discussion which hon. members may wish to have on this question. It is an important question and it would naturally have come up, and will naturally come up, this afternoon when the Minister of Veterans Affairs brings his estimates before the house; but to ask the government to accept a motion which will mean, if carried in this house, the defeat of the administration itself at this time is asking much more than can be expected of any administration.
Having said this much may I say that I have been looking carefully at the wording of the second part of the motion, and it is to the effect-
. . . that the government should give immediate consideration to the amending of the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act so as to provide increases in the basic disability pension, the war veterans allowance, and the allowance to veterans' widows and orphans, to enable those receiving these pensions and allowances to meet the increased cost of living.
What is asked for there is immediate consideration of the matters that are therein mentioned. I have never found the government unwilling to give consideration to all important matters, and certainly the government would not be unwilling to give consideration to the matters that are referred to here. But if hon. members mean by immediate consideration that the cabinet must meet, that the Minister of Finam e must reconsider

Pensions and War Veterans Allowances
estimates in relation to what may be required for these purposes, and that we shall have to wait here, if any action is to be taken, until' the approval of His Excellency is obtained to a resolution to be brought before the house and a bill introduced, it is unreasonable to expect the government to take that step at this time.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), that support of this motion would be a vote of want of confidence in the government. speechtext:
I have sent for the volume. It is not here yet, but my recollection is that I am entirely correct. There is an immediate problem before us now and that is the welfare of these men who today find themselves in the position of receiving a matter of less than S31 a month. They find themselves in difficulties and they ask that parliament do something, and- not run home when matters such as this are before the house. Immediate consideration of an amendment to the Pensions Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act so as to provide increases for the basic disability pension is sought. If the Prime Minister will rise in his place and free his membership on the other side of the house in a vote such as this, I believe the majority of them will support this amendment so that war veterans allowances and the allowances to veterans' widows and orphans may be increased to meet the increased cost of living.

When the war veterans allowance was first introduced it was in the form of an application of the old age pension to veterans at the age of sixty. At that time we recognized that veterans were pre-aged by ten years; therefore the very least that should be done is to immediately increase the amount of the war veterans allowance to the highest old age pension paid in this country, which at the present time is $40. That is something which should be done at once. It will not be satisfactory; it will not be enough, but at least it should be increased to $40, which is the amount of the old age pension paid in Ontario. I say this because we recognize that the war veterans allowance is a federal responsibility. The government cannot shove it off on the provinces. In view of the fact that the war veterans allowance is an application of the old age pension, certainly we should increase it to the amount of the highest old age pension paid in any part of this dominion.
There is another unfortunate thing about the war veterans allowance. Today it is being used for the purpose of giving an allowance to a soldier who in reality is entitled to a pension. Instead of paying the pension we pay the war veterans allowance, which of course means that the amount of money paid is far less than the amount of the pension would be, and at the same time we do not guarantee the same security for the dependents of the veteran. In addition, of course, the means test is involved in the war veterans allowance, whereas the means test does not apply in connection with the pension.
I am not going to say more on this matter at this time, but when the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs come up we shall have more to say about the various measures coming under that department. I

On previous occasions I have left veterans affairs to the younger men who fought in the last war, but this matter affects my buddies of a previous day, the widows of many of those men, and those who are unemployable, between fifty and sixty years of age. I feel very strongly on this question, and I feel ashamed of the House of Commons today that politics should be brought into the consideration of this matter. This is something for the benefit of the men who offered their lives for us, and it should be kept on a much higher plane than that; yet here we have sunk to such a level that we are discussing matters of elections in connection with it.
People are suffering today in an attempt to live on S31 a month. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) said anyone supporting this amendment would be hurting the veterans. I can assure my right hon. friend that I have never hurt any veterans and never will; but I am supporting this amendment. I belong to the legion, and I have dozens of branches in my constituency. I have here a letter from the legion that has not yet been placed on record, and I am going to read just two paragraphs, because I know time is very valuable today. That is something worth while for this government to look after. Then the letter concludes with these words:
We would, therefore, ask you to make this cause your own, so that the matter shall be dealt with before parliament prorogues.

The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has placed us in the position that whether or not we might have felt the purpose of the amendment had been served, we must now ask for a recorded vote of this house.
The resolution is very simple. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) said it was an amendment to the budget. It is nothing of the kind. If you will look at the resolution you will see that it merely states:
This house is of the opinion that the government should give immediate consideration to the amending of the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act so as to provide increases in the basic disability pension, the war veterans allowance, and the allowance to veterans widows and orphans, to enable those receiving these pensions and allowances to meet the increased cost of living.

After all, in April of this year, due to the policy of the government in removing controls, the cost of living jumped almost two points. In May the cost of living increased almost to the same extent. In fact the cost of living has risen sharply over the last few months and indeed since the end of the war. Consequently, having reached this point in the session, I think we are justified in asking that this be done, since no provision is being made anywhere in the measures now before the house, as far as we can tell, for meeting this very urgent situation. So I say that since the Prime Minister has thrown out the challenge we cannot do other than accept it.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, I have just a word or two to say with regard to this amendment. It has been said that the government has been very generous, more generous than any other government in the world, and that may be true. What I regret is that the government has been generous to too many people, and there has been no complaint from anyone in the opposition when outsiders were given the preference in regard to everything. Therefore I find not that the government has not been sufficiently generous but that it has been too generous to one class of people. That is why the cases of some of our own soldiers should be adjusted.
The amendment asks for increases: first, in the basic disability pension; second, in the war veterans allowance; and third, in the allowance to veterans widows and orphans. It is not a question of increases to all but a matter of adjusting some pensions and allowances which have not been fairly established by the department. My great objection to the Department of Veterans Affairs is that it is a department where wrongs are not redressed; and they are not redressed because the minister seems indifferent to what goes on in the department. When my hon. friends speak of the high cost of living, it is true. Why is it so? It is the old story; it is on account of taxes. Why do we have taxes? We have them because of expenditures. When we were protesting against some expenditures running into billions of dollars all my hon. friends of the Conservative party, of the C.C.F. group and of the social credit group voted for those expenditures. I do not see how they can oppose government policy when they vote for increases in taxes, for increased expenditures and for increases in the cost of living.
Moreover, I cannot understand the logic of other parties which put candidates in the field against the government candidates.
[Ma. Coldwell.]
We had a by-election in Halifax and I remember saying to one of my good Conservative friends-

Every hon. member has been speaking of the high cost of living. If you look at the amendment you will see that it has the cost of living as its basis. First, pensions are mentioned; second, allowances are mentioned and, third, allowances are mentioned again and it is said that they should be increased in order to meet the higher cost of living. The opposition parties are not logical in putting candidates up against the government and in opposing government policy in the house as they are doing by this motion. I am explaining what it is.
They are opposing government policy in the house today. This is the same thing as happened during the by-election. They all vote with the government on the main issues and then afterwards those issues are contested in the different elections. They seem to forget the votes they have cast in the house in support of government expenditures because they criticize them afterwards when they go to the people. They say, "This should not be done, that should not be done." How can they do that? As sensible men how can they swallow everything in the house and vomit it up outside the house? That is what they are doing all the time. When some hon. members try to protest against expenditures it is useless. It is always good to spend money.
We now have the results which were foreseen for a long time by a few of us. We were called all sorts of names because we spoke our minds. We supported a wholly Canadian policy, a policy that would put Canadians before all others. How is it that our returned men and the widows and orphans of ex-service men cannot get'enough? It is simply because we have put foreigners, strangers and outsiders on an equal basis with those who served in the Canadian army, and sometimes we give them preference. That is why I objected to it.
I do not think the remedy is in an amendment like the one brought forward by the hon. member of the C.C.F. party. They are surprised when someone speaks to them in the language of common sense and shows them how they are acting contrary to their former votes. I can do that because I voted against it, but those who voted for it cannot

Pensions and
War Veterans Allowances
do it. I have the right to do it and I do it, not with joy but with regret. I should be delighted to err but I cannot.
I have no sympathy whatever for the Minister of Veterans Affairs and I do not think he deserves any. I appreciate the stand taken by the Prime Minister when he said in his own language that he was not going to be blackmailed by anyone, that he wanted to wait for the opportunity to make an announcement. That is the language of a leader. His policy is not going to be dictated by those who vote against it in the house, by those who belong to other groups. He should listen to his own supporters. He should draft his policies after consulting his own supporters. How is it that a young Conservative member gives a lecture to the Prime Minister because he has not answered properly a question put before the house by the C.C.F. group? The Prime Minister used the language of Asquith: he said, "Wait and see."
A lot has been done for the returned men, and I do not think they can complain. There are some wrongs which should be redressed; probably 10 or 15 per cent, but the soldiers have been well looked after theoretically. Some credit must be given to the government. I tell my hon. friends that I am not concerned about an election. If an election occurred tomorrow I would be in the hands of my electors. If they vote for me I shall be proud to represent them; if they vote against me, I shall return home and make more money with my law practice.
The question is not one of an election. The problems of the soldiers, the veterans, and their widows and orphans should not be made a political football. The last reason why I am bound to oppose this amendment is that I am anxious to get on with the estimates. I shall not say one word more. I want the estimates right away.

Right Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs): With the consent of the committee I wish to make a brief introduction to the presentation of the estimates of veterans affairs, which have been ready for over three months. It may be of assistance to hon. members if I make this brief statement regarding veterans affairs as a whole. The figures which I shall quote include the supplementary estimates which were tabled a few days ago. These aggregate $4,925,000, almost entirely for hospital and other treatment purposes.
The estimates now before the committee for all activities of the Department of Veterans Affairs for the fiscal year 1947-48 aggregate $450 million. The total estimates for 1946-47 were $749 million. The decrease is $299 million. These figures include statutory items as well as items to be voted. They also include, in addition to normal government services, the amounts required for loans and investments. A very large amount of the

decrease is due to the fact that the payment of war service gratuities is now very nearly completed. There are also substantial reductions under a number of headings as follows:
Treatment and pension examinations for world war II		$21,000,000
Post-war discharge rehabilitation
benefits	  24,230,000
Hospital accommodation and facilities	    13,000,000
Grants to veterans settled on provincial lands	 1,000,000
Grants to Indian veterans settled
on reserve lands	 1,000,000
However, Mr. Chairman, largely because of an increase in the number of veterans entitled to war veterans allowance and to pension, there are certain votes in which the estimate for 1947-48 is greater than the estimate passed last year. We have been able to reduce the requested appropriations for all administrative items other than those related to the payment of pensions and war veterans allowances. Increases in these two items are directly related to the increased number of veterans who will be receiving benefits under this legislation.
While there is a very substantial reduction of $299 million in the estimates for the Department of Veterans Affairs this year, it is appropriate that I should assure the committee and the country that this reduction is due entirely to the fact that certain services and payments related to the demobilization period are very nearly completed. These reduced expenditures do not reflect any impairment in the high standard of services which parliament has authorized for war veterans. There is not, and there shall not be, any falling off in the quality of services which this country has rightfully insisted shall be available to former members of our armed forces.
I want to say a word about pension and to give a fairly graphic picture to the house. The total amount provided in the 1947-48 estimates for pensions for both world war I and world war II, is $80,750,000. Our appropriation for 1946-47 was $74,750,000, and the actual expenditure was $70,748,000. On May 31, 1947, there were 181,200 pensions in force representing an annual liability of $70,725,000. The pension liability is increasing at the rate of approximately $800,000 a month in Canada. Our estimated expenditures under this head for 1947-48, are based on the belief that this rate of increase will continue throughout the fiscal year.
I come to the question discussed earlier this morning of war veterans allowances. Let me give just a few facts. The four votes

Supply-Veterans Affairs
providing for funds necessary to meet payments on account of the allowances authorized by the War Veterans Allowance Act total $14,480,000. Our estimate for 1946-47 was $14,180,000 and the actual expenditures were $12,000,000. On May 31 there were approximately 31,350 allowances in effect representing an annual liability of approximately $14,750,000.
It is necessary, sir, to provide funds to meet the liability we have under the act, although from actual experience we usually find that the full amount is not required because of the fact that recipients receive and report other incomes thereby permitting a reduction in the amount of allowances payable. There has been a steady increase in the amounts payable under this act for several years, and it is expected that this trend will continue owing to the fact that veterans of world war I are now entering the age at which they will be entitled to receive benefits.
Coming to the important question of treatment, the department's medical treatment services have been raised to a very high standard and have received commendation from many sources, especially one from Winnipeg the other day, from the Canadian Medical Association. During the fiscal year 1946-47 it was necessary to expand our treatment facilities rapidly to ensure that veterans might receive treatment of the high standard to which government policy entitles them. The several votes, including the supple-mentaries, providing funds necessary for the department's treatment services covering operation of hospitals, payments of allowances to veterans receiving treatment, and construction of hospitals, total the very great sum of $65,300,000. The decrease this year in our treatment service is $31 million. The actual expenditure was $78 million last year. Our hospital facilities are being improved and modified as rapidly as possible under present conditions, and the estimate of $10 million for this purpose represents our anticipation of the extent to which during the current fiscal year we shall be able to carry on with the construction of new hospitals, extensions to existing institutions, and modernizing the present premises.
It will be necessary during the year to close a number of hospitals which were opened primarily to meet the peak load during the demobilization period. These hospitals are being closed only after the number of patients reaches such a low figure that continued operation of the hospitals is not justified, and then only when other facilities for proper treatment of veterans are available in the area concerned or in adjacent areas.
In regard to benefits, a study of the department's estimates will show that provision is being made for the fiscal year 1947-48 to the extent of $94,850,000 for post-discharge rehabilitation benefits. This compares with the 1946-47 figure of $96 million, although our estimate last year was $119 million.
During the current fiscal year many veterans will reach the end of the period during which they have entitlement to certain benefits under the veterans rehabilitation act. This applies particularly to out-of-work allowances and in a lesser degree to vocational training. It is expected however that expenditures on account of "benefit awaiting returns" will continue at a high rate as veterans become established in their own businesses and upon farms.
Expenditures on account of university training are expected to reach a peak during 194748 at a sum in the neighbourhood of $39 million. The amount required for this purpose will, however, decline in future years as veterans complete their courses or cease to have entitlement to assistance. It has been gratifying to observe how remarkably well student veterans have done in their courses at the several universities across the whole dominion. They have ranked high among the winners of scholarships and prizes in our Canadian universities. I am confident, Mr. Chairman, that as a result of what this parliament has done, the contribution of these veteran graduates to the welfare of Canada will be such that the expenditure in training will always be regarded as one of the most profitable investments this country has ever made.
There is, sir, cause for gratification in the fact that the contributions to the unemployment insurance fund on account of veterans is continuing at a high rate. The significance of this fact is that the veterans of Canada are finding their place in the industrial life of this country. The Veterans Rehabilitation Act provides that when a veteran has spent approximately three months in insurable employment the Department of Veterans Affairs shall pay into the insurance fund a sum equivalent to the contributions which would have been paid had the veteran been engaged in that employment during the period of his service in the armed forces. Up to March 31, 1947, contributions amounting to $10,280,000 aad been paid on behalf of more than 136,000 veterans. We estimate that we shall require $15,000,000 for this purpose during the present fiscal year.
I now come to gratuities. This is what the people of Canada have done. Payments on account of war service gratuities to which

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Supply-Veterans Affairs

speechtext:
veterans are entitled under the War Service Grants Act had reached the total of $453,350,000 on March 31, 1947. That is what the people of Canada have done, and rightly done, for those who served during the war and saved us. The amount paid during the last year was more than $221,000,000 for war service gratuities alone. Those moneys are paid over to the veteran in a series of monthly instalments immediately following his discharge. We now find that these payments have very largely been completed. This is a statutory item and only a fragmentary percentage of the original liability remains unpaid.
We did something else in this parliament, and we were the only country in the world that did it; I refer to reestablishment credits payable over a period of ten years. The amount of credit entered up to the account of veterans under the War Service Grants Act is slightly in excess of $365,000,000, which they can use for ten different purposes decided upon by this house in its wisdom. The amount to which veterans are still entitled as shown in the books is $191,000,000. Under the terms of the legislation this amount is available to them at any time within ten years from January 1, 1945, or the date of the veteran's discharge, whichever is the later date. The extent to which payments may be required during the coming year is impossible to estimate with precision, since it depends upon the impulses of possibly several hundred thousand veterans. The item is statutory. In making up the estimates we have thought it wise to count on a somewhat heavier demand during 1947-48 than was experienced last year.
Just one word on the Veterans Land Act. We have discussed it many times already during this session, and possibly I should not say much more. The settlement operations under the Veterans Land Act have now reached large proportions. The point I want to leave with the committee is this. We had some trouble with our housing, as hon. gentlemen know, but the larger operation has been tremendously successful. Up to April 30 of this year, qualification papers have been issued to 63,535 veterans. Loans and grants had been approved to a total of $128,746,308.
Just at this point may I ask if the minister has the figures as to the veterans who have actually been settled?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No. I will get them. These were applied as follows: 14,817 farmers, $70,300,058; 10,990 small holders. $56,833,696; 427 commercial fishermen, $1,612,554. That makes a total of 26,234 veterans who had obtained financial assistance under the

Veterans Land Act up to April 30 last. It is expected that by the end of the present fiscal year this number will be over 35,000. The veterans established under the act are meeting the terms of their agreements with complete satisfaction. For the last fiscal year-and I wish the committee would note this-95-2 per cent of maturities were paid by our settlers on the land; that is, world war II settlers. Repayments, including initial deposits, totalled $12,068,297. It will be observed that the appropriation asked for in connection with the administration of this act closely approximates the sum voted last year.
That, sir, is a synopsis of the activities of what I believe is today the largest department in this government, a department which, I may say, has received the kindly support of every party in the house, and certainly from my colleagues and my leader it has received the most marvellous and inspirational encouragement. If after thirty years in parliament I shall find it necessary to leave active public affairs, I shall never be so proud of anything in my life as of the work I was privileged to do during the last twelve years for the ex-servicemen of the Dominion of Canada.
Mr. WHITE	(Hastings - Peterborough):
This morning I suggested to the minister that there should be a standing committee on veterans affairs, and this afternoon I understood the minister to say he was in favour of such a committee. I wonder if the minister would go a bit further and say he will have such a committee set up early next session.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As the Prime Minister said, no single minister makes a decision on behalf of this government, but it is my intention to recommend to my leader and my colleagues that we have a committee next year.

I thank the minister, and I know if he recommends it we will probably have a standing committee of the house on veterans affairs. It is hardly necessary to review the work of the veterans affairs committee during the two years it sat. As I said this morning, however, if this committee had been set up this session probably the motion and debate that took place today would have been avoided. Many times since last session the agitation on the part of various veterans' bodies in regard to the basic rate of pension must have been brought to the attention of the department. It has been brought up in the house many times and has been very actively discussed, particularly since last session, by branches of the legion all over Canada. I have noticed

Supply-Veterans Affairs
press comments and reports covering large sections of this province, indicating that various branches of the legion have passed resolutions to be forwarded to the minister advocating an increase of from 25 per cent to 33J per cent in the basic rate of pension. Before the minister's estimates are through I should be very glad if he would make some statement as to his attitude or feeling in the matter of an increase in the basic rate of pension, which rate I understand was set about 1920 and has not been increased since.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me I should like to give him the figures, and they very largely bear out what he has just said. In 1925 the cost of living index was 119-8. In 1939 it was approximately 100. On March 1, 1947, it was 128-9, and on April 1, 1947, it was 130-6. The increase between 1925 and 1947 was 7-6 per cent. The increase between 1939 and March 1, 1947, was 28-9 per cent, and the increase between 1939 and April 1, 1947, was 30-6 per cent. The annual pension liability, as I said, was $70,000,000. The cost of a 7-6 per cent increase would be $6,000,000. The cost of a 28-9 per cent increase would be $23,000,000.
Perhaps while I am on my feet my hon. friend would permit me to give the corresponding figures with regard to the war veterans allowance. The cost of living index in 1930 was 120-8. In 1939 it was approximately 100, and on March 1, 1947, it was 128-9. The increase from 1930 to 1947 was 6-7 per cent; the increase from 1939 to 1947 was 28-9 per cent. The annual war veterans allowance liability is $14,000,000. The cost of a 6-7 per cent increase would be $938,000, and the cost of a 28-9 per cent increase would be $4,046,000. War veterans allowances have been increased from $20 to $30.41, an increase of fifty per cent, or more than the increase in the cost of living from either 1930 or 1939.

I thank the minister; but when he got up I thought he was going to give us his attitude or his feeling toward an increase in the basic rate of pension. The figures he gave as to the increase in cost of living may be very interesting, but personally I have not much faith in the figures as to the cost of living as shown by the bureau of statistics, because I believe any housewife in Canada, no matter in what part of the country she lives, will tell you in no uncertain terms that the cost of living has increased far more than is shown by the figures issued by the bureau.
The minister said the veterans allowance had been increased from $20 to $30.41, an increase of 50 per cent. I would say to him 83166-3671
at once that when the allowance was fixed at $20 it was far too low. The fact that there has been some slight increase, even though that increase amounts to 50 per cent, does not mean that the rate being paid today is at all adequate. The situation becomes more marked when you compare soldiers' pensions to old age pensions. As the minister knows the rate of old age pensions has greatly increased; and in Ontario, the province with which I am most familiar the mothers' allowance, workmen's compensation and similar allowances have been increased over the years. Surely the minister would be the last to say that the basic rate of pension or veterans' allowance should be lower than the allowance paid by any other department or any province. This morning I mentioned briefly the case of the widows of pensioners with a disability of fifty per cent. My understanding-and if I am wrong I hope the minister will correct me-is that on the death of a fifty per cent disability pensioner his widow will continue to receive something like $40 to $60 a month as a pension. If the pensioner has a disability of less than fifty per cent his widow will receive no pension, unless she comes under the provisions of the War Veterans Allowance Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If I may correct my hon. friend, just to keep the record straight, in the first case mentioned the widow is entitled to a pension of $60 a month.
That is where the disability is fifty per cent or more?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Correct.

I am quite in agreement with that. There must have been some reason for fixing fifty per cent as the point of division, but it seems to me that when the husband dies the widow is more than ever in need of a pension, and should be entitled to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is fixed at fifty per cent because then there is a presumption that death was due to service.

I will not quarrel with that, either. But on even more than compassionate grounds I would say that if during his lifetime a man was in receipt of a pension of only five per cent or ten per cent or anything up to fifty per cent, on his death the widow should be entitled to more than she receives now, which I believe is something like one-third the pension which was paid to her husband. If the department realizes and admits that the
Supply-Veterans Affairs

widow is entitled to a pension at all I cannot understand why, after the death of the pensioner, his widow should not be entitled to an adequate pension without having to apply under the War Veterans' Allowance Act, in which case she is met with this most unfair means test. I hope the minister will make some statement on this point which I consider to be very important.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I interrupt again? I am just trying to be helpful. If death is due to a disability attributable to service, then usually a pension is granted.

At this late date, as far as the veterans of the first war are concerned, you will find that the members of the pension commission are as hard as the granite which comes from the land where the minister comes from.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the pension commission are very kind-hearted people.

I should like to mention a matter which came up on June 9 when the Minister of Finance had his budget resolutions before the house. This had to do with part of the reestablishment credit which is paid to a veteran attending university. The details may be found on page 3942 of Hansard. I referred to the case of a married veteran attending university who was receiving $60 per month-say he receives $60 during the university period. His wife is working. The Minister of Finance told me that in computing the amount of income tax payable by the wife she would deduct from the $600 the veteran received an amount of $250, and all over the $250 would be deducted from the exemption of $1,500 allowed to the wife and she would pay tax accordingly.
The Minister of Finance pointed out that this particular wife was not supporting her husband because the husband was getting the allowance. I tried to point out to the Minister of Finance on that occasion that this was not a matter of a husband receiving income or salary, that the student veteran was actually receiving a part of his reestablishment credit. As I understand it, no part of a gratuity, reestablishment credit or any benefit received because of war service is taxable in any way.
I understand further from the Minister of Finance that a student veteran who took a job during the summer and earned $500 or $800 or whatever it might be would have to add to that amount the $600 he was receiving as a reestablishment credit in computing his income tax. If that is so, I think it is most
(Mr. G. S. White.]
unfair to the veteran. The minister knows that many representations were made in the veterans committee that the $60 a month was not sufficient. If the minister knows anything about conditions in Toronto as far as board, transportation and other things are concerned-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It would be $80 a month.

In this case the wife was working and he got only $60. I think the minister will find that it would be most difficut to get along on $60 a month. I heard the minister refer once in the veterans affairs committee to the time when he went to school. I agree with him because I know when I went to school $60 would have been a great deal of money. Unfortunately today in Toronto, and I think this would apply to practically every university town, $60 a month is quite small.
The veteran should be encouraged to take employment during the summer in order to earn money to help him through the next year. He must also provide for the time when the allowance of $60 a month will run out because his period of entitlement may be only twelve months or so. If what I say is correct and if the explanation given by the Minister of Finance is correct, many of the veterans attending university are going to be sadly disillusioned about the $60 a month they are getting.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend most sincerely for his observations. I shall renew my investigations of the situation which he has described.

I appreciate what the minister has said but I think he should go farther. These men will be taxed for their earnings in 1946 and they will be subject to tax for this year. The minister may recall the item which appeared in the press of yesterday that tuition fees at the university of Toronto were being increased by at least twenty per cent. I will leave it at that and hope that the minister will make an investigation into this unfortunate matter. If he finds the facts are as I have stated them I hope they will be corrected.
Just a word about the pension commission which the minister says is very kind-hearted. I have never found them to be that way. The minister will recall that the old question of preenlistment disability came up at many meetings of the veterans affairs committee and was the subject of discussion along with the question of the benefit of the doubt. Can the minister assure the committee that the

pension commission are dealing fairly with the veterans in connection with preenlistment disability?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I happen to know every member of the pension commission. They are all men who served; they are comrades of my hon. friend: and of myself. I know how sympathetic they are. The chairman is present and I know how sympathetic he is to the 'type of case mentioned by my hon. friend. I can assure him that every sympathy and consideration will be given to preenlistment conditions.
Mr. WHITE OHastings-iPeterborough): That sounds very nice if that is actually the way it works out. I should like to explain what often happens. When a veteran is up before this kind-hearted pension commission he is often faced with his medical sheet or other records and he is shown where he answered a question asked by a doctor or some other examiner. That answer probably referred to a difficulty that occurred many years ago but we find this kind-hearted pension commission instantly pouncing on that one point and taking the position that whatever the present disability is, it is due to a preenlistment condition which was not aggravated by war service.
In many cases information is obtained from the soldier in connection with these matters in a rather unfair way. He is not told that anything he says may have some bearing on a claim he might make for pension in the future. When these cases are taken up a letter comes back from the pension commission relating the condition to something back in 1932, 1935 or in the 1920's. It is stated that in the opinion of the medical officers of the pension commission that is responsible for the present condition. If a pension is granted it is on a small scale because they claim that practically the whole disability is dlue to something that happened before enlistment. The medical examination of any soldier who joined the army in 1942 was a great deal stiffer than the examination the minister and I went through in 1914. The soldier was examined thoroughly in every way by specialists. Every part of his body was examined, and he was X-rayed, and it was pretty difficult to put anything over. The soldier got a more thorough examination than he would get if he was applying for a policy of $5,000, $10,000 or $25,000 from any insurance company in Ontario. I say to the minister again that after the soldier has had this most thorough medical examination and has been accepted in the army with A-l category, anything that happens to him after
that should be attributed to his war service irrespective of what the kind-hearted pension commissioners may say, irrespective of what documents the- medical officers of the pension board may sign, and a pension should be awarded1 to the soldier on the basis of his disability.
At -the conclusion of his remarks the minister referred briefly to the Veterans Land Act. I for one would like the minister to make a further statement on veterans housing, which is a very important matter, not in any one isolated spot but across the whole dominion.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A complete and comprehensive report on veterans housing has been prepared and is now available, and when we come to that item I shall be only too glad to table it or to let any hon. member of the house have a copy of it. It deals with every single project in every province in the dominion and1 with what has been accomplished, and the general conclusion of that report is that the repairs will be completed at the end of this month of July. Would the minister make a statement on one further matter which I brought before the house some two or three weeks ago in regard to the Veterans Taxi Owners Association of' Montreal? At that time I understood the minister to say that an investigation was being made or a report was being obtained, and I rather expected that following that the minister would make a statement to the house. I noticed a press dispatch from Montreal dated yesterday which stated that Major Ferland, formerly with the Department of Veterans Affairs, had been before the court on that day and that one Colonel Hay of the Department of Veterans Affairs had made the statement that at the time this taxi association was formed Major Ferland was an official of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and further that many of the veterans involved in this taxi association had called at Major Ferland's office in the Department of Veterans Affairs to pay their fees. I hope the minister will also tell the committee whether or not he favours and will advocate an increase of the basic rate of pension and the rates under the War Veterans Allowance Act.

speechtext: la regard to the first question, I have received a report, -which I have not under my hand but of which I shall be glad to send my hon. friend a copy, in regard to the Veterans Taxi Owners Association. There are two angles to the situation, with which I was not very familiar. In regard to increasing the basic pension, that ^ is a matter of government policy which will be considered during the recess and wifi be further considered by the special committee on veterans affairs, I hope, which will be set up early next session.
Would the minister say he was sympathetic to recommending an increase in the basic pension? Surely he will go that far. He can only speak for himself.

Mr. Chairman, it is approximately one year ago that the veterans committee completed their work on the veterans charter, and I think generally speaking, we all felt that we had completed a pretty good job in so far as the programme of rehabilitation for the veteran of world war II was concerned. But the minister will remember that many members expressed a good deal of dissatisfaction with the programme for the veterans of the two wars. We realized that there was no chance of a veteran of the two wars being able to take advantage of the Veterans Land Act on account of his age, and we also realized there was not the opportunity for the older veteran to get employment today in competition with younger men. However, while we were generally satisfied with the programme of rehabilitation for the veteran of world war II, we were not by any means satisfied with the pension bill which was submitted to the house. The minister will remember that the pension bill which was submitted to the house last year did not represent the unanimous view of the members of the veterans committee. It did not even represent the will of the majority of that committee. As I said this morning it merely represented the will of the government as put forward by the Minister of Veterans Affairs. As I intend to deal with this subject at some length I shall refresh the memory of the house as to what took place at that time.
A draft bill was submitted to the veterans affairs committee, and- we spent many days and weeks considering that draft. Finally we completed a bill that did receive the unanimous approval of the members of that committee on every main point. Then we held meetings in camera and the minister told

us that the government was not prepared to accept the amendments we had made to that draft bill, and in view of the fact that the amendments we had moved would have involved an increase in expenditure the minister had the power to veto those amendments. It will be recalled that some of the Liberal members of the committee then substituted a number of amendments, and as there was a sufficient number of Liberal members on the committee to force those amendments through, they carried. Therefore the bill submitted to the house was a bill that represented the opinion of the government rather than the opinion of the veterans committee. It is important to keep that point in mind, because from time to time we are going to hear in this house that that bill was recommended by the veterans affairs committee. That bill did not represent the majority opinion of the members of the veterans affairs committee. I remind the committee of that, because until the amendments we originally made to the draft bill are incorporated in the Pension Act and until certain other undesirable features are dealt with I am afraid that many veterans will fail to get a square deal under the Pension Act.
Two of the main points at issue were the insurance principle, which was reinstated in the act, and the question of cases of preenlistment origin. There is still a good deal of dissatisfaction on that question. The figures given to us at that time were that at the end of December, 1945 , 7,810 men had been refused pensions on the grounds that their disability was of a pre-enlistment origin. These men had1 served overseas, were classified as fit on enlistment and had been discharged as unfit. Many members of the veterans committee have come in contact with veterans who they found had been severely penalized as a result of that ruling. The great majority of the committee were of the opinion that an applicant's condition as recorded at the time of enlistment should be presumed to be his actual condition. I remember that the hon. member for Vancouver South moved an amendment along that line and it received the support of the committee but later on was ruled out. Further, in that connection we were of the opinion that any subsequent deterioration during service should be recognized as the result of that service and consequently a veteran should be pensionable for that impaired condition unless that condition had been recorded prior to enlistment. We had already struck out the words "wilfully concealed". However, as I say, the government was not prepared to accept that amendment.
