A change was made in the section dealing with the benefit of the doubt, and in the present act that section is section 62, which I shall read. It is supposed to give the veteran the benefit of doubt. It states:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension, the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall be entitled to draw and shall from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
But as I shall show later on, apparently cases still come before the pensions commission in *which the veteran does not appear to receive the benefit of the doubt. Furthermore if the pension commission feel that even though they give the veteran the benefit of the doubt they are not able to award a pension there is another section under which the pension can be granted on compassionate grounds for meritorious service. I refer to section 21. Section 21 reads:
The commission may, on special application in that behalf, grant a compassionate pension, allowance or supplementary award in any case which it considers to be specially meritorious, but in which the commission has decided that the applicant is otherwise unqualified to receive such an award or supplementary award under this act.
With sections 62 and 21 one might argue, surely the interests of the veterans are fully protected. When we were discussing this matter in the committee we were asked to wait and see how these sections, or section 62 as redrafted, worked before going any farther. But section 62 does not appear to carry very much weight with the pension commission, and the commission seems to be loath indeed to u,se section 21. It seems to me that the Department of Veterans Affairs invariably uses the war veteran's allowance to take care of such cases. It must be remembered that the war veterans allowance does not provide anything like the same amount of protection that the pension does. In the first place the amount is less; in the second there is a means test applied to the war veteran's, allowance, and in the third place the dependents of a pensioner are protected to a far greater extent than under the war veterans allowance.
When the veterans committee sat in 194546 its whole time was taken up with work on the charter. We knew very well that if we started to deal with individual cases we would have so much work on our hands that it would bog down and we would never complete the charter. Therefore it was agreed that at that time we would not deal with any individual
cases. But as I have already mentioned, when dissatisfaction was expressed the minister suggested that we should wait for a year to go by and see how the charter as it is now constituted worked out in the interests of the veterans. A year later many feel that there are certain sections of certain acts that should be amended, and at the present moment I have especially in mind the Pension Act. I should like the minister to say whether it is his opinion that when the veterans committee is set up next year-I understand that he is going to try to set up the committee next year-it would not be possible for that committee to make a new departure. I think that committee could act as a kind of board of review to deal with individual cases to see just exactly how the veterans charter is working out in actual practice. I suggest that the various veterans' organizations throughout the country be allowed to bring forward their strongest cases. Then we could act as a kind of board of review to see whether or not the charter is working in their interests, and if we were satisfied that it was not, the government should be prepared to pass the amendments which are necessary to make it work better.
The minister knows that in the past it has never been my practice to recite individual cases in the house. Personally when I brought cases before any branch of the Department of Veterans Affairs I have received every consideration; but on the other hand the number of cases with which we can deal are limited, as the minister knows. I think he will agree that it should not be necessary for any veteran to bring his case before a member of parliament. He should be able to receive the same satisfaction by bringing up the case himself as when he brings it to the attention of a member of parliament, and it does not seem to me that that was always so. Therefore at this time I wish to cite the case of one old veteran who I believe has failed to get the benefit of the doubt or to be dealt with as a meritorious case. While I do not like to take up the time of the committee at this stage of the session, I think I am justified in taking a fair amount of time to recite the case of John V. Thom, M.M., 21st battery, C.E.F., in the war of 1914-18. His regimental number is 86684. I may say that this case was referred to me by Mr. Walter H. Kirchner, M.C., D.C.M., a veteran of 1914-18. Whem Mr. Kirchner brought that case, to my attention I asked one or two people just what kind of organization the Canadian Combat Veterans Association was. They stated that it was not a very strong organization and did not represent a very large number of veterans.
Supply-Veterans Affairs

Therefore I mentioned that fact to Mr. Kirchner and I received this letter which in fairness to Mr. Kirchner I think I should place on record to show what backing Mr. Kirchner has in bringing forward this case and others at this time.
Dear Mr. Quelch:
In view of the fact that the representations I am making concern the well-being of certain classifications of the disabled men of two generations of combatants, may I cite other more powerful numerical groups who by their actions vouch for my bona fides. The Canadian Combat Veterans Association Incorporated was formed in the year 1937, and we are now in the eleventh year of our history as an organization whose work is confined to one particular sphere, namely, the implications of the Military Pensions Act where its democratic administration is concerned.
Our charter is granted under the Societies Act of British Columbia. Our membership under the charter is confined definitely to the men (and women) of world wars I and II, who have actually seen service in the forward areas of war. We have no "honorary" membership, neither do we canvass membership. Those whom we admit have to be recommended by our membership, and we are very particular in this regard to see that our charter is not violated.
Regarding funds from other sources:	In the
year 1941, when I gave evidence before the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs, the dominion command of the Canadian Legion, through their president, asked if they could make a donation towards the expenses of our representations, which was accepted and acknowledged by letter. The dominion command of the Army and Navy Veterans' Association, Inc., also made fairly substantial donations at the same time, and subsequently their provincial command, in British Columbia. Donations have also been received from units of the Canadian Legion, both in Vancouver and throughout the province. Donations have also been received from other responsible veteran groups-all unsolicited, as our records will testify. Copy of the letter passed to you, from the pension adjustment officer of the Army and Navy Veterans Association, in British Columbia (Mr. J. H. MacLeod), is a more recent contribution from one of the numerically powerful veteran groups. The latter donation is important because the representative of the unit concerned is undoubtedly one of the ablest advocates in the dominion on the military pensions legislation.
The donations which have been made to us as an association from the two senior and numerically strong veteran groups is due to the fact that some of the vital matters I have presented to the membership of the House of Commons require specialized knowledge of the legislation in certain spheres, and my position in this regard, as the secretary of the Canadian Combat Veterans Association, is generally accepted among veterans' associations throughout the dominion.
As to my personal status, the brochure of April, 1947, which is in the hands of the membership of the House of Commons, makes this clear.
Thanking you, . . .

And so on. I want to refer to the letter which he mentions as having been written by Mr. J. H. MacLeod, secretary of the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans' Association of Canada. This letter reads:
Dear Comrade Kirchner:-I have for acknowledgement your letter of the 12th, with enclosures, for which many thanks.
It is pleasing to note that your latest crusade has reached its culminating point. Let us hope that you will again be successful in extracting further concessions from those in the seats of the mighty for the amelioration of our deserving comrades in distressed circumstances.
The necessity for drastic revision of the Pension Act and treatment regulations becomes more apparent every day.
We now have on our hands worthy veterans of both wars: men with meritorious front-line service, in many cases pensioned for wounds, who are refused treatment for neuro-psychosis, epileptic and other conditions which, on any reasonable construction, must be referred to the stress and strain of war. These men are being thrown on relatives, or on the community at large, for treatment and maintenance. All too many are finally relegated to mental hospitals (insane asylums) because of the department's obstinate stand in these matters. Surely the time has arrived when something must be done to remedy these obvious defects in our Pension Act and in its administration.
I quoted that letter to show that Mr. Kirchner, in bringing forward these cases, does not represent merely the Canadian Combat Veterans' Association, but has a great deal of backing from the Canadian Legion and the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans' Association of Canada.
Coming back to the case of Mr. John Thom, this man enlisted on November 12, 1914 in the artillery and served overseas in the 21st, battery, C.F.A. He went to France on January 18, 1916 and served in France until December 29, 1918. He saw action for the first time on the Ploegsteert front, was awarded the Military Medal for action on Vimy Rjdge, was buried by the explosion of an ammunition dump, and saw service at Passehendaele, Amiens. Arras and on the Drocourt-Queant line. He was discharged in Canada on April 5, 1919, after three years service in France and four and a half years altogether.
I would like to read to the bouse Mr. John Thom's medical history as given by himself. I could put it in my own words but I think it is better to read his own statement so that no one can accuse me of having distorted it in any way. Here is an example of a man who enlisted in a good state of health, having a strong physique. He bad a splendid war record and then failed to get a square deal. Let me read the medical history of Mr. Thom, from 1919 onwards:
First I want to point out that at no time has there been any dispute regarding the extent

Supply-Veterans Affairs
of my sickness, and that since November, 1928,
I have been regarded as 100 per cent disabled; in fact, when my financial circumstances, six years ago, made it necessary for me to apply for the war veterans' allowance, it was only a matter of form granting me the same. (2) At my date of discharge, April 5, 1919, my medical history sheet shows that I had defective hearing of the right ear, caused by my being in an explosion in the summer of 1917-which left me unconscious for hours, and damaged my inner ear. (3) One month after discharge I went to work with the C.P.R. dining car department, running from Vancouver to Winnipeg. On these trips I began being bothered with severe headaches and dizzy spells; and of course my hearing was bad. As these spells became more frequent I called at the Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment (S.C.R.), and asked them to check over my ear. The doctor's report was that there were scars on the ear drum, but that not much could be done about it. As time went along these spells became more frequent, and much more severe, until in the summer of 1925-after one severe attack, in which I became unconscious, the ear became badly infected and started to discharge. When I reported to Dr. De Muth, the C.P.R. doctor, he sent me to Dr. Grant Lawrence, the ear specialist. As my ear was in such a bad state it eventually affected my eyes. (I have now almost lost the sight of my left eye.)
(4)	By this time I found I was unable to carry on with the C.P.R., so I got leave of absence and went into the hotel business, in Vancouver, for myself. Although I was making a nice return out of the business I eventually had to sell out as the noise and excitement connected with the hotel business seemed to aggravate my head condition.
(5)	About this time (1927),! was still attending Dr. Grant Lawrence, with my ears and eyes. As the trouble seemed chronic I decided it was a matter for the pension board. My complaint was headaches, dizziness and deafness. In a very short time I was granted a 10 per cent pension for otitis media, retroactive to my date of discharge.
(6)	By the spring of 1928 I thought I was a little better and took a job as sales manager for the Dominion American Industries Limited, but as soon as I started to work I began getting worse again, having to miss every other day at work; and although the company was very nice about it, I could see that it wasn't fair to them, so I resigned in November, 1928. It was at this time, on applying to the Pension Department that I found out my mistake: in my ignorance of medical terms I thought that otitis media included my whole head condition, but I was informed that it was only the hearing, and that was what I was pensioned for, and not the headaches, etc.
(7)	Eventually they decided to give me a hearing, at which they decided to give me a five per cent increase for otitis media-but that the cause of the headaches, etc., was neurasthenia. As I had been in Shaughnessy hospital several times, and nothing seemed to be done for my head, a friend of mine made arrangements for three of the leading specialists to examine me and find out the source of my trouble; the three specialists were: Dr. Des Brisay-Diagnosis specialist; Dr. F. Emmons, brain specialist; Dr. Grant Lawrence, ear, eye and nose specialist.
(8)	As their report made it clear to me that my ear condition was the cause of my headaches and eye trouble, and that it was the headaches that were the cause of the neurasthenia, I asked the department to give me a hearing in front of a quorum.
(9)	Eventually the hearing was held with Colonel Cy Peck, V.C., and another gentleman sitting on the board. At the hearing, as you will see by the evidence on file at Shaughnessy, the three doctors when asked if the otitis media was the cause of the headaches, etc., they definitely stated, "Yes"; and Dr. Emmons explained in detail how the headaches were caused.
Colonel Cy Peck, V.C., seemed so convinced that when we asked to cross-examine the departmental doctors he said that would be unnecessary-as there was no room for argument. You can imagine my surprise when I received the decision from Ottawa, when they did not even mention the specialist's evidence, but stated that some Doctor Baillie of Christie street hospital, Toronto-who had never seen me, or examined me-had decided that my headaches were not caused by my ear trouble-and so the board decided not to give me any increase on my pension.
As I thought that the court reporter might have made some mistake in taking down the evidence, I went up to Shaughnessy, and as I am not allowed to see my file personally, 1 asked Mr. Derby, district administrator, if he would mind reading the evidence, as I was sure there was some mistake somewhere. But the evidence was correct, so the slip must have been somewhere else. Of course, knowing Mr. Derby's official position I didn't embarrass him by asking his opinion, but I could see he was just as surprised at the board's decision as I was.
After that, I applied to the appeal board, and asked to be notified when it would come up at Ottawa, so that I could have someone to represent me. They agreed to do so, but the first thing I knew, the case was over, and as far as I know I wasn't represented by anyone.
There is just one more item that I would like to draw to your attention: it is regarding the War Measures Act, which doesn't allow any pills which contain any ingredients required for war purposes given for non-pensionable disabilities. As I get the pills for my headaches, I was notified; but as soon as I showed Doctor Jones at Shaughnessy, Doctor DesBrisay's report, he immediately notified the dispensary that I was entitled to the pills, and to fill my prescription. Now, I don't think that if a man of Doctor Jones' standing, after reading Doctor DesBrisay's report, comes to the decision that my head trouble comes from my pensionable disability, that a Doctor Baillie of Toronto- who has never seen me-is qualified to pass an opinion in the negative with the same evidence in the matter of my pension.
The whole point that I think is so unfair is that the board took the evidence of one doctor, who had never seen me, against three specialists, who had thoroughly examined me. And, if their evidence hadn't been as conclusive as it was-I was still entitled to the "benefit of the doubt" clause in the Pension Act, which my war record certainly entitled me to.
I should like to refer to the evidence of these three specialists to whom Mr. Thom refers in his statement. The three specialists
Supply-Veterans Affairs

mentioned were: first, Doctor W. F. Emmons of Vancouver. According to the evidence given to the Canadian pension commission in 1938, Doctor Emmons was a graduate of McGill, 1924; three years on staff of McGill, physiology, and five years at Mayo clinic studjdng neurology. Practised in Vancouver for past six years-that is, years prior to 1938. Examined patient J. Thom in 1935. I shall read only the opinion of Doctor Emmons at the end of his statement. It is as follows:
It is my opinion that this man is suffering from intermittent attacks of severe vertigo due to inflammatory irritation of the right vestibular apparatus, which are a definite and integral part of the former right otitis media, for which he is already being pensioned. It is quite probable that the neurosis and headaches are attributable to the fear of the attacks of vertigo which, in turn, are definitely connected with his otitis media.
Then, Doctor Grant Lawrence, Vancouver, according to the evidence submitted to the Canadian pension commission in 1938, was a specialist, eye, ear, nose and throat; graduate McGill, 1917; post-graduate work, New York, Vienna, London; sixteen years' practice Vancouver. In his statement, and again I will just give the final paragraph, he states:
All hearing tests indicate a chronic otitis media, probably involving the inner ear and bony labyrinth. His attacks of iritis and headaches are suggestive of a foci of infection, and I would consider his ear as the probable cause.
The last specialist was Doctor DesBrisay of Vancouver who, according to the evidence submitted to the Canadian pension committee in 1938. is a specialist in internal medicine; graduate McGill, 1917; after overseas service in 1919, one and a half years' internship at Vancouver and Chicago; two years in Mayo clinic in medicine; three years Lockwood clinic, Toronto; five years assistant professor of medicine at Dartmouth, New Hampshire; practised internal medicine, Vancouver, for past eight years-that is for eight years prior to 193S. Here is his statement, and again I just read the opinion at the end of it:
Opinion:	Chronic otitis media, with labyrinthitis and associated headaches.
I believe that this man's headaches are due to the ear condition. I would advise extraction of the questionable tooth, because of the history of iritis. I do not think that the tooth could have any bearing on the headaches.
There you have two of the doctors saying that the headaches are due to the condition which is pensionable, and the other doctor saying that in his opinion the headaches are probably due to that cause.
It is interesting to note that the appeal board which granted Mr. Thom's application to have his case reopened drew special atten-
[Mr. Quelch.l
tion to the evidence of these three specialists. The decision handed down by the appeal board in January, 1945, states:
The appeal board doth order that this application be granted.
The members of the appeal board were J. K. Matheson, H. A. Bridges and R. J. Gordon. Then under the heading of "Reasons for decision" we find this, and I will just read the last paragraph, unless the minister wants me to quote the whole statement. The last paragraph reads:
While, in some respects, this application is one which might be dealt with on a "consequential" basis by the Canadian pension commission, the board has finally decided that a prima facie case for leave to reopen has been made out, particularly having regard to exhibits 36 and 37, in the summary of evidence, and the evidence of Doctors Grant Lawrence, H. A. DesBrisay and W. F. Emmons, at the quorum hearing.
The application for leave to reopen is therefore granted.
Then the pension commission wrote this letter to Mr. Thom after his case had come before them:
Ottawa, August 9, 1946.
Mr. John Thom,
3852 West 29th Avenue,
Vancouver, B.C.
The commissioners have reviewed your application for entitlement in respect of Nervous 'Condition.
After careful and sympathetic consideration of the evidence and record before them they are regretfully of the opinion that the condition has no relation to your service, and therefore, it i3 not pensionable. Their decision follows:
The applicant served from November, 1914 to April, 1919, with service in France.
He is in receipt of pension at the rate of twenty per cent for chronic suppurative otitis media, incurred during service. He is now claiming in respect of nervous condition.
There is no reference to any nervous condition during service, or post-discharge, until 1927. The commission is not able to find evidence to connect this condition with service, and rules

Nervous condition-not attributable to service.	*
R. Simpson,
Assistant Secretary.
The commission apparently completely disregarded the evidence of the three specialists giving his nervous condition as a pensionable disability. I think it is of special interest in view of the fact that the appeal board definitely drew the attention of the pension commission to the evidence of those three specialists. I have in my hand a letter which seems to have a bearing on this matter. It was written by J. Z. Taylor, chairman of the Canadian pension commission, dated Nov-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The decision has been made, and this just brings up the question of what little progress we can make if we take up individual cases. This gentleman was given the right to apply for a second hearing, and these things naturally go ahead in the ordinary course of events. If we are to try to review every single pension case I do not know when we shall get through. The hon. member has already spoken for forty minutes. I do not want to make any complaint about that, but I suggest that other hon. members know of cases which they have an equal right to bring up and read to the committee at much greater length. The hon. member also knows that these matters are confided to a judicial commission, and that this has been done with the idea that there should be no interference on the part of the government with the commission. He also knows that the minister has said he will recommend that a committee be set up next year which can look into all these individual cases. In the light of all this; in the light of the decision rendered in this particular case, which shows that these matters are going through in the ordinary course of events, and since the hon. member has taken forty minutes to deal with a case in which entitlement has been granted in the ordinary course of events, I appeal to the hon. member to let these items go through. Then, if he does not think these matters are being dealt with properly he may take them up before a committee which can deal with them much better than they can be dealt with in this house.

I have been in the house since 1935, and this is the first time I have brought up an individual case. We spent two years in drafting a charter for the veterans. Many members of the committee expressed the opinion that the Pension Act was not
satisfactory, and that veterans would not get a square deal under it. We were told to wait for a year to see how it would work out. I am giving as an example a case in which I consider a man has not received the benefit of the doubt under section 62. It is all very well for the parliamentary assistant to say this case has now been dealt with, but this matter has been under consideration since 1927. How long does a veteran have to wait to get justice? This case was first brought up in 1927, and now we are told the man may receive a pension. The granting of entitlement does not necessarily mean he will get the pension he should get. It does not necessarily mean he will get a pension for the full disability; we have to wait and see the attitude of the pension commission. I realize that since I have spoken for forty minutes I can continue only with the unanimous consent of the house.

Did John V. Thom, M.M., No. 86684, 21st Battery, Canadian Field Artillery, enlist in the 1st great war, November 12, 1914, at Regina, Saskatchewan, classified physically AX, with no mental or physical defects; age twenty-two?

(a)	Persistent, severe headaches
(b)	Dizziness and vomiting

In view of tlhe file I have read-I 'have a very full file here from which I have just read briefly-it does seem to me that section 62, giving the benefit of the dou'bt to the veteran, apparently means nothing. Further, it seems to me 'that section 21, which provides for compassionate grants in meritorious eases, is not- being observed by the pension commission.
