speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I shall take only a minute of the committee's time. My hon. friend raised four points. The first point which dealt with section 62. which is the benefit of doubt section, and section 21, which is the meritorious award section, will be dealt with briefly by my parliamentary assistant. May I point out to my Ihon. friend that dual war veterans have aid the rehabilitation treatment and pension entitlements available to world war II veterans. In addition they have special entitlement under the War Veterans Allowance Act whereby service anywhere qualifies them. They have class 6 treatment or domiciliary care under the meritorious service clause.
There is a special officer at D.V.A. head office to render service and advise on any problems affecting them, and there are special counsellors and interviewers in each D.V.A. district office. There are special officers who pay attention to their employment needs at each regional office of U.I.C., Department of Labour, national employment service. There has been a dominion-wide campaign under way to obtain reserved jobs in industry for older veterans and 'they also receive a preference in 'the corps of commissionaires by virtue of age.
I should like to say a further word about the second point raised by my hon. friend, that of employment for older veterans. In order to assist older veterans to obtain employment, the Department of Labour and voluntary agencies throughout the country were asked to support a campaign for the employment of veterans of fifty years and upwards. Full cooperation was obtained.
Now for the figures. Veterans with service in both wars who were registered as unemployed on April 1 numbered 9.262. New registrations in April and May were 7,611. This gave the aggregate registrations to May 31 as 16,873. Those who found employment in sixty-eight points only through our activities and those of the Department of Labour numbered 9,399. Since this last figure of those placed in employment does not cover all registration points in Canada, it is evident that approximately 10.000 older veterans successfully found employment during the first two months of the campaign. The number now registered as in search of employment has been materially reduced, notwithstanding the 7,611 new registrations.
We are greatly indebted to the many agencies, mostly voluntary, who set up 'this amazing record by successfully attacking the myth that older veterans are not a good employment investment. We intend to continue our work along these lines, because large numbers of the veteran population of Canada will reach the over forty-five age mark each year for the next twenty-five years. I think we are travelling along the right lines.
The third point mentioned by my hon. friend was the question of the charter. We shall be only too glad to examine how effective has 'been the work of the great committee which sat last year in bringing about re-establishment reform for our exservice men. That can easily be included in the terms of reference to that committee.
Supply-Veterans Affairs

As his fourth point he raised the case of John Thom. This veteran's champion has abused me pretty bitterly, and he has abused one of the best friends the returned soldier ever had, the hon. member for Vancouver South. I do not think I will say any more about that. I should like to get the advice of >the medical men in this house, because I know nothing about medioine myself except what I take occasionally. This is a most involved case. The hon. member's long dissertation has been rendered unnecessary by the fact that- entitlement has been approved and assessment will be established. I think I have dealt with all the points raised by my hon. friend.

I think the minister will agree that it has taken a long time because the case was first raised in 1927. It should not be necessary for a veteran to have to wait for eighteen years in order to get a square deal. I am very glad to hear that even at this late day the case is going to be dealt with satisfactorily; at least I hope so.

I shall not be as long as my hon. friend because he said a great many things with which I agree, neither shall I attempt to deal with everything in the veterans estimates with which I should like to deal. I am sure that other hon. members will be dealing with some of these matters and there is no need to repeat. I should like to deal with something that specifically comes under this administration item.
Before I do that, I want to refer to a statement which the minister made today. I want to assure you Mr. Chairman, that while I am physically hot and uncomfortable there is no emotional heat in me. I am not going to be critical or set myself up as a judge. I am simply going to state a case and ask that something be done about it.
I want to remind the minister that while what he said was substantially correct, that the veterans committee did agree on the final draft bill and agreed at that time that this was the report of the committee, we also agreed with the minister that when the matter came up in the house one member from each party would state his party's view briefly. I at that time was chairman of the caucus committee of the C.C.F. and made the statement on behalf of our party. The statement I made was this, that we would not offer any further criticism of anything that was done by the committee or the government, but. we would watch the operations of the veterans charter and reserve the right to bring to the government's attention at. the next session, meaning this session, any things that we felt 
were not working out properly. I am proud of the humble part I had in the preparation of the veterans charter and I want to give credit to the government and to the minister, who has, I believe, an expansive sympathy and a good heart for the veterans, for the things that they have done. He and the government deserve a tremendous amount of credit, and I am proud of being a humble citizen in a nation that is willing to subscribe to these things.
I assure the minister that I shall make no comparisons between Canada and. any other country. I am not interested in a comparison between what Canada is doing for her veterans and what some other country may be doing. I am simply interested in what Canada can do for her own veterans as well as her own citizens and do it willingly and gracefully, as she has done these things willingly and gracefully, and I am proud, as I say, to be a humble citizen of such a country.
Before I go further, I want to pay a tribute to the minister and his departmental officials. In the few individual cases that it has been necessary for me to take up with the department on behalf of some veteran., I have received nothing but courtesy and help, and in every case where the condition complained of could be corrected within the framework of the act, that was done. Unfortunately one or two could not be corrected and, when the next veterans committee sits, amendments will have to be made to the act to permit the officials to correct these conditions.
Having said that, I think everybody, including the minister and his officials, will recognize that we would not be a human society if, no matter how carefully our veterans legislation or any other legislation were drafted, certain individuals at some time, in fact quite frequently, who claimed benefits under the act did not feel that they were not getting the treatment they should get, and the officials would be less than human if they claimed that in every case where dissatisfaction arose the applicant was wrong and the official was right. That would be a kind of society we cannot yet visualize. So I want everybody to realize that in what I say this afternoon I am. speaking in no spirit of criticism whatever. I am not being critical and I shall not attempt to judge. I am simply going to state a case.
I shall give an individual case, but it is a key case typical of a small group of people who were prisoners of war in Japan. I shall not read the whole deposition. In order to save the time of the committee, I shall summarize it.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the hon. member be kind enough not to give names, but to give the initials and regimental numbers.

I am sorry I have not the regimental numbers. This is the case of Armourer Sergeant T. O. Jacobson, of the Royal Rifles of Canada, first battalion, C.A.SE. The case was submitted to me by Mr. Walter Kirchner, secretary of the Canadian Combat Veterans Association. I also have the letter written by Mr. Kirchner to the hon. member for Acadia, which has already been read to the house and which it is not necessary for me to read again, except to say that in the citations which Mr. Kirchner makes as to the veterans organizations which have supported him, I cannot entirely overlook the evidence submitted by Mr. Kirchner on behalf of his organization, even though that evidence may conflict with that of the officials of the veterans affairs department. I am not judging who is right or wrong; I am simply saying that the evidence has sufficient weight to merit attention.
Briefly, this is t'he history of Armourer Sergeant T. O. Jacobson's case. He joined up in the summer of 1940 at military district No. 12 in Regina. His medical examination was thorough and proved him to be in the highest medical category. He went to Saskatoon for training and from there to Valcartier and then to Quebec city. In October, 1941, he had completed his training in the Royal Canadian Ordnance Corps and was attached to the Royal Rifles of Canada as Armourer Sergeant. He left with the Royal Rifles of Canada for Hong Kong shortly afterwards. I am sorry I cannot give his regimental number.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have it here on file. It is L-50094.

At Hong Kong he took
part in the resistance battles at Suymun, Tai Tam Yap-we heard something about yapping the other day-Wanchai, Chek-i-wan, Chico, Pal, Villa, Stanley Village, Repulse Bay and Fort Stanley. I am a little more at home with the last three names.
On December 23, 1941, he was wounded in the right leg and left wrist and, while trying to reach an ambulance service, he was 'blown over a ridge by shell fire, landing on a rocky ledge twelve feet below. If you fall twelve feet onto a rock you do not have to be wounded or blown by shell fire to be hurt. You are badly shaken, even though you are in the best of health. Two days later, along with other survivors, he was made a prisoner of war of the Japanese. From then on, his history was one of disease, hard work, ill treatment by his captors, and near starvation,
with little medical attention. In his deposition he goes into that in greater detail, but I am trying to save the time of the committee and I assure hon. members that what I am stating is in line with the soldier's deposition to me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I wonder if I might
interrupt the hon. member. This is a case very much like the last one in which the pension commission carefully considered the symptoms and came to the conclusion that the man was very likely suffering from amoebiasis-I may not have pronounced it right, but everybody knows what it is.
Say it in English.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Amoebic dysentery, a
tropical disease which naturally is not common in Canada and which, if the diagnosis is definitely confirmed, entitles the man to pension according to his degree of disability. This is another case that has been going through the ordinary course of procedure by the pension commission, and demonstrates again that we can, if we wish, spend a great deal of time in discussing these matters on the floor of the house. But it does not have so very much effect, because. these matters are being considered as best they can be by the commission under the ordinary machinery and procedure which are set up by parliament. I mention that because it may shorten the hon. member's remarks.

I will be just as brief as I can. Unfortunately the parliamentary assistant did not touch on the exact point I want to get at, because I cannot do it until I go a little bit further into this history. That is the reason I am making the summary. However I am glad to be assured by the parliamentary assistant that this man's case is actually being dealt with. I am afraid that, while it may not be too late, it is later than it should be.
I want to go on with this little summary. After the war, this man was repatriated, of course, and landed in Victoria in the fall of
1945.	That was nearly two years ago. He was given his first forty-two days debarkation leave, but had to go back to the hospital at the end of thirty days. From then on, it has been a succession of in and out of hospital and on and off work. Late in October,
1946,	a year afterwards, he went back to Shaughnessy Heights hospital and was given check-up tests by a psychiatrist. In this particular check-up-I must refer now to the man's actual statement and point out the things that are objectionable-the features that appear to be objectionable to this man and his
Supply-Veterans Affairs

sponsors-and, if true, I think they would be objectionable to most of us-are these.
He says:
I was given to understand that it was more a case of what he-
He is referring to the psychiatrist, -described as emotional instability; that we Hong Kong men more or less imagined we had these pains, aches and feelings of numbness, and that by now we should be well recovered from our past conditions and ailments. That is not only happening in my case but in other Hong Kong prisoner of war cases. We are told now that we are only suffering from a case of nerves, and that, in spite of our complaints to the contrary, our condition is good, in spite of our sore backs, stomach upsets, sore, burning, and aching feet.
He goes on a little bit farther, but I shall not give it all.
These same doctors do not seem to realize that the Japs spent four years doing everything in their power to break us down by starvation, exposure, brutality and beatings, and aided by all kinds of diseases and plagues; and, under those conditions we are supposed to have made a comeback to physical fitness in the period of twelve months.
That is the key part of the objection that this man is making, and if he is correct I think he is making a justifiable complaint. That does not indicate to a layman like myself that, now the commission have discovered he has this particular type of disease which was mentioned a few moments ago by the parliamentary assistant, that can be the only disability from which a man who went through that experience would be apt to be suffering.
If the man's statements are true, I feel, and I am sure other hon. members must feel, that there is something more which can be done for this man than to treat him as he claims he is being treated. He goes on to say further:
About the middle of January, 1947, I was approached by Dr. Margetts to take the pyn-thotol test . . .
This, I understand, is a truth serum, and he claims now that he did not want to take it. He claims that he insisted that that particular kind of test was given only to murderers or suspected murderers who are being given a severe examination. He claims that, by refusing to take this test, he was cut off immediately from insulin treatment. If that is true it is a serious charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: By whom, by our department?

Yes, by the hospital authorities at Shaughnessy Heights or wherever the psychiatrist was doing his work. That is what he claims. He goes on to say:
I was boarded by Dr. Palmer.

Then he goes on to say:
I was weighed by Dr. Palmer, wearing at the time full army battle dress, boots, underwear, shirt and heavy socks.
He claims that the doctor put down his weight without counting the weight of his clothing, and told him that he was gaining in weight, although he had not gained nearly as much as he should have. At that time he claims he was also told by Doctor Palmer that he had recovered from all the ailments and vitamin deficiency, beri-beri, pellagra, malaria, dengue fever, dysentery, diarrhoea, jaundice, back ailments, bad eyesight, loss of weight, sore, aching and burning feet; tightness of muscles and cords; lack of sense of balance. He says he was discharged from hospital and pronounced cured in April, 1947, but still claims he is unfit.
The parliamentary assistant has just told us that the case is being considered, but something must have happened to get the case considered if the man concerned states the case correctly up to April. As I say, I am not trying to judge whether he has stated it correctly or not, but I am saying the case is too serious, and the charge as made in the long depositions is too serious, to be lightly passed over. Even if there is a partial element of truth in it, the man should have more sympathetic treatment from the departmental, medical and other men who are working in that particular hospital.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I interrupt for a second. Is it not more important to get entitlement and assessment at once? We could then have a committee of this house go thoroughly into any suggestion of impropriety in regard to treatment.

In the main, I think I can agree with what the minister suggests there. I could cite a lot of other cases, but I am not going to do so because I do not think it would be fair to the committee, and I do not think it is of any use. I just want to mention this to the government. In the light of these and many other charges which have been made by Mr. Kirchner, secretary of the Canadian Combat Association, I suggest to the government that they should be investigated. When I say that I want you to know, Mr. Chairman, and the minister to know I am extremely jealous of the honour and position of the officials of the department. I would hate to have a false charge made against them by anybody in this country. But as I said, the weight of evidence here indicates that a lot of people feel there is something in these charges, and some veterans-

Supply-Veterans Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt, but I think Mr. Kirchner came before our committee in regard to certain other statements that he had made. I did not say a word in regard to these, but the committee dealt with them.

I am trying to be helpful and not take too long. I have a great admiration for the work that is being done by the department. I do not want to see any official or the minister himself charged unfairly, but when we get the kind of statements that have been made in these charges it is bound to have an effect on a lot of citizens and veterans in this country and raises a certain amount of-if not actual doubt-of question in the minds of some of the rest of us. I believe that some kind of investigation or hearing should be held so that these people who are charged would have an opportunity publicly to state their position and to clear themselves of these charges.
I am simply anxious to have the minister look into the matter at once. I do not think it should be left to a parliamentary committee next session to bring these people here. The matter should be cleared up immediately, either by a small committee composed' of all the parties in the house or by a completely independent committee, so that we can get the public denial properly. The minister and his assistant have the denial, but I have not got it where I can take it to a legion branch and lay it before them. I think the public should have it. I am not making charges, nor am I spreading charges on the. record. I think that, in the interests of all concerned, the matter should be cleared up, and if there are guilty parties they should be isolated and removed from positions where this kind of thing can be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As far as we are concerned, I would welcome a committee of three doctors from this house to go into the suggestions that have been submitted, and I would suggest the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) and the hon. member for Inver-ness-Richmond (Mr. McGarry). They could meet sometime between now and the next session and call in whom they want and submit a first-class report.

That is quite a concession for the minister to make and I appreciate it, but I would ask him to go one step farther and include a member from this end of the house-because we have no doctors-to consider the layman's point of view.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Absolutely, yes.
If the minister says he will do that, I have nothing further to add except thank you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I appreciate what the hon member for Swift Current has said about clearing up the charges that have been made, and the minister's suggestion is a good one because it would enable us to have the matter clarified. The department is determined that these prisoners of war shall be properly looked after, and they are called in every six months for examination, whether they apply for pension or not, to make sure that there is nothing wrong with them, for which they might be entitled to pension. In this particular case, the reason Mr. Jacobson has obtained his entitlement is attributable not to complaint, but to that policy. Regarding all these cases of Mr. Kirchner, the investigation head of the Canadian combat association, and the Canadian pension commission has taken up thirty cases with him. He has intimated that there are twelve others he wishes to take up. Whenever he wants to take them up with the pension commission they are prepared to go into them with him.

As a war veteran and a former member of the veterans affairs committee, I take a great and particular interest in the Department of Veterans Affairs. I wish to say a few words on this item this afternoon. In fairness, I think I should say that the Minister of Veterans Affairs has a warm heart, which occasionally, perhaps, causes him to commit verbal indiscretions in the house, but at the same time it has been responsible for his taking a broad, human and sympathetic interest in the welfare of the veterans of the country.
In my opinion, the Minister of Veterans Affairs, during his term of office to date, has rendered a great service to the veterans of Canada and has been a great credit to the office he holds as well as to the present administration. In addition to that I should like to express my appreciation of the courtesy I have received from the officials of his department, and of their great interest in the cause of the veterans. There are some departments of the government that could well take a course in human relations from the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I have had occasion to take up a number of cases with the various departments, and I have found the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs most cooperative and painstaking and given to the examination of questions in the greatest detail in order to find a satisfactory solution of the problems that confront them.
i

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I am not going to take up the time of the committee this session to go into details regarding the many matters I should like to discuss. I support whole-heartedly the proposal made for an increase in pension rates and for increases in war veterans allowances, the arrangements with respect to widows, and further advantages to merchant seamen. I support whole-heartedly all the proposals made today and on previous occasions.
I believe the Canadian people are willing to pay for these increased benefits that are being advocated1 at the present time, but we must at the same time be prepared in 'this house to support a budget that will pay for these increased costs to the government of the country. Might I suggest what I would do if I were minister of finance; because, of course, I could never be minister of finance. My wife says that- I am a poor chancellor of the exchequer. If I were minister of finance, however, I would bring down my budget with alternative proposals.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think you would make a very good minister of finance.

I would place before the house a budget to provide for the payment of old age pensions, war veterans allowance and pensions on the present terms, but I would also have alternative proposals that would allow for the payment of pensions on a scale advocated by the members-in some cases advocated by the members of all parties- and then we should have in crystallized form something that could foe placed squarely before the house so as to ascertain whether the house was willing to vote a budget to pay these increased costs.
I am happy to hear there is to be established next session a committee on veterans affairs to deal with these problems. I am sorry it was not set up this session, but if it is set up next session and these various proposals are brought before that committee, evidence should be heard from those advocating them, and I am sure that in a cooperative, non-partisan spirit, such as has been shown in these matters in the past, a satisfactory solution can be found which we can place before the house and the people of the country.

There are one or two observations I should like to make, one of them being in connection with the overseas fire-fighters. Last year I had something to say on this question. To me it is stupid that the overseas fire-fighters are denied the civil service preference. I know of several cases where these men have applied for positions with the government as fire-fighters and

have been denied the chance to secure them because they had not the overseas civil service preference. That is not businesslike. I do not think it is either economic or sound, from a business point of view, that a professional fire-fighter should be denied a job with the government in his chosen profession on such a ground as that.
There is another matter I wish to take up. I refer to girls who served overseas with the Canadian Red Cross. If my memory serves me correctly, nearly every member of the veterans affairs committee was of the view that the Red Cross girls who served overseas should receive all the privileges accorded other auxiliary services. The presentation of a brief representing their interests was done without their knowledge and was grossly inaccurate. That was presented on July 15, 1946, I think it was, last session before the veterans affairs committee. On that occasion, Major-General Browne and Mr. Norman S. Caudwell, K.C., presented that case. I believe Mr. Caudwell presented the case. He seems to have greatly misinformed the committee. I presume the department have received this brief. Mr. Caudwell stated that many of the girls, especially in the first period of enlistment, were from well-to-do families. As a matter of fact, of the draft of eighteen girls to go overseas, fifteen gave up positions from which they earned their living. There was another thing which Mr. Caudwell stated which was not accurate. He said they served as voluntary workers and that, while overseas, for pin-money they received from the Canadian Red Cross $30 a month. They did not receive S30 a month. They received twenty-five shillings a week, which amounted to something less than $30 a month. They received $260 a year in Canadian funds.
Mr. Caudwell also stated that they received $150 allowance to buy civilian clothing, which they did not receive. Actually each girl was given thirty days' leave with pay on her return to Canada, and that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend, just in order to be helpful?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If and when the committee is established next year the cases to which he refers-the Red Cross and the others-will be considered by the committee.

That helps things a good deal. I shall now be through in about a minute. I am pleased to hear that statement from the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and I am sure that these people will receive justice.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

I just wish to take three or four minutes to put before the minister a particular case. I do not intend to go into any detail, but there is a point which I should like to make. This is the case of Frank W. Connorton.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What is his number?,

Regimental No. V-52017. This is a case of spinal fusion which appear? from the evidence to have resulted from a technical error in administering a spinal anaesthetic at the time of an appendectomy performed in June, 1943, while Connorton was in the naval service. He had evidently enlisted in January, 1943. The claim is made by the department that Connorton's condition is of pre-enlistment origin. The validity of that claim has not been established so far as I have been able to determine by scrutiny of the evidence. The details of the evidence, together with two affidavits which I have in my possession, completely refute the department's claim and seem to substantiate the contention of the veteran that his injury was sustained while he was in service; and further that his present helpless condition is a direct result of the medical bungling at the time of his appendix operation. I should like to read this one Short affidavit which was supplied by the Vancouver Engineering Works. It reads as follows:
To Whom It May Concern:
Re Frank Connorton
I wish to state that Frank W. Connorton worked with me in his capacity as an apprentice machinist, from the year 1941 up until the time he left the employ of the Vancouver Engineering Works to enlist in the R.C.N.V.R.
His duties as a machinist called for the physical stamina of an able-bodied man at all times; in fact, from his activities here I have always considered him physically well above the average fellow employee engaged in this class of heavy lifting work.	_
Frank Connorton was a cheerful, willing and able worker, well liked, as those who were his fellow employees can testify.
Yours very truly,
Vancouver Engineering Works, Ltd.
William Dalglish,
Machinist.
That certainly testifies to the physical condition of the man prior to his enlistment. Within months after his enlistment, an appendectomy was performed. At the time of that operation a medical student jabbed his back eight times with a needle before he could achieve anaesthesia, and the man suffered after effects; at least, that is his claim. Evidently he feels aggrieved. This is the point I should like to make. The Minister of Veterans Affairs has been eminently fair in
handling the situation here this afternoon; and I believe I must compliment him on some fine work done in his department. But if a man such as Connorton feels he has a case for damages, I wonder if it would not be possible for the minister to grant him a fiat to sue the crown and establish his case in the exchequer court where evidence can be taken under oath. It seems to me that would be a good way of disposing of a case such as this. I would ask the hon. minister if he would not take that suggestion under consideration and possibly give this man a fiat to sue.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question, for information purposes?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Has this man appealed his case to the existing organization, the Canadian pension commission?
Yes. I understand that the disabled veterans association has taken up the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But has he appealed to the pension commission?
I do not know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That procedure would not cost him anything. I should be glad to recommend to my colleague, the Minister of Justice, a fiat to the exchequer court, but I think the other procedure should be tried first.
I think that is wise and that, if he has not tried' it, he should.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would my hon. friend be kind enough to check that?
I will check that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I have a report here, according to which there apparently was one Canadian pension commission ruling on May 10.
1947.	Of course he would have the further right of appealing, and so on. There, all his expenses would be paid and everything like that. That would be much better than going into court.
Very well. _

I was sorry when earlier today, on the amendment which I introduced, the Department of Veterans Affairs was brought into the discussion. It was not my intention to bring it into the discussion at that time. I must say that as far as the Department of Veterans Affairs is concerned, and as far as the minister is concerned I, like all other members of the house, have always received every consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Thank you very much.
Supply-Veterans Affairs

The cases which I have brought to their attention have been dealt with promptly; much more promptly probably than cases are dealt with in a great many other departments of the government. I think the minister has his department well organized. I do not altogether agree with him in his argument with regard to there not being a necessity for the raising of our pension basis at this time. He quoted figures from 1920, showing that the cost of living at that time was as high as or higher than ait the present time. I agree with that. The cost of living was higher at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: When pensions were stabilized in 1925, they were slightly higher; but I think the figures which I gave here-I have not them in front of me at the moment -show that there was a tremendous increase in the cost-of-living index between 1939 and 1947. I was trying to make out my hon. friend's case for him.
I must have misunderstood the minister. I thought he was arguing the other way.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: When my hon. friend reads Hansard tomorrow, I think he will find that what I say is correct.

I am glad to know that the minister's argument was as he has stated it. I would also bring to the attention of the committee that today our whole Canadian standard of living is higher than it was ten, fifteen or twenty years ago. I think we all enjoy a better standard of living today. We have more cars, more radios, more refrigerators and more of the other amenities of life than we had then, and it is only fair that the pensioners and others should enjoy these things with us. So I think there is a good argument for increasing certain of these pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I be permitted to interrupt to repeat what I have already said today. According to the information given me, the cost of living index in 1919, at the time of the first bonus of twenty per cent, was 126-5. In 1920, at the time of the second bonus of thirty per cent, it was 145-4. In 1925, as my hon. friend knows very well, the bonus was included in the scale of pay, and the cost of living index was 119-8. From 1935 to 1939 it was around 100. On March 1, 1947, it had gone up to 128-9. The increase from 1925, when the consolidation of the bonus was accomplished, to 1947 was 7-6 per cent. Then these are the figures I want to emphasize. The increase from 1939 to 1947 was 28-9 per

cent. The annual pension liability, based on this year's estimates, is $80,750,000, including both wars. The cost of an increase of 7-6 per cent would be $6,232,000, and the cost of an increase of 28-9 per cent, representing the increase in the cost of living from 1939 to , 1947, would be $23,698,000. Is that quite clear now?

Yes, it is; and I think the people of Canada would be quite willing to spend any additional amount necessary to give our men and women who went overseas the same standard of living that is enjoyed by the rest of us. I think that is the principle behind all the veterans legislation, to deal fairly with them and see that they may enjoy the same things we enjoy.
I should like to say just a word in regard to the setting up of the veterans committee I have been one of those who believed that should be a standing committee of this house, not a committee just set up at the pleasure of the government from year to year, or in certain years when they might feel it necessary to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I again interrupt my hon. friend, in a desire to be helpful? There is another virtue in that suggestion. In addition to reviewing legislation from year to year, that committee could deal with the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs. There was some criticism this morning to the effect that those estimates were too long delayed. They could be considered by the committee and completely disposed of, as they were practically disposed of last year. That is another virtue to the suggestion made by my hon. friend.

I am afraid the minister is making my arguments for me on most of these matters. As I was saying, I have been one of those who believed there should be a standing committee of the house on this matter, and I think probably the government are going to move in that direction. I hope so, anyway; and I hope that when we come back next year this committee will be set up. From what has taken place in the house today, the need for such a committee is quite evident. I think the Department of Veterans Affairs have exercised genuine care in trying to secure suitable personnel, but today they have some eight thousand people working for them in all parts of the dominion, many in executive positions. It would be humanly impossible for them to be able to choose that number of employees who would reflect the opinion of the department itself. People are bound to come into the department with ideas of their own, ideas at variance with those of the members of this house and the

Supply-Veterans Affairs
members of the veterans committee which drafted this veterans charter. So in a standing committee of the house those matters can be talked over, and I believe that committee can be of great assistance. I do not think it should be a committee to criticize. This morning the minister more or less accused me of introducing a resolution for political purposes. That has not been my object since coming here, and I do not think I can be accused of doing that either in this house or in any committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I interrupt
again? I have the highest respect for my 'hon. friend, as I think I said this morning. What I stated then was that the possibilities and implications of the resolution were such that it might be construed as being possessed of political purposes or political motives, because it was a straight vote of confidence on a matter affecting the veterans.

I can assure the minister
that the motives were perfectly honest as far as I and this group were concerned.
The minister has been agreeing with me so much that I think I shall introduce another subject and see if he will agree on that. In my estimation there was perhaps one weakness in the veterans charter. It is not a matter of vital importance at the moment, but it will become such within a few years. That is the matter of the education of the children of deceased veterans. No doubt many of these widows will marry again, and the time will come in the not too distant future when the matter of the education of these children will have to be dealt with by this parliament. I hope that in the veterans committee next year the matter can be discussed and some measure provided under which the children of deceased veterans will be able to take advantage of what would have been the rights of their parents had they lived. I believe that suggestion is only fair.
When the minister was dealing with the operations under the Veterans Land Act and the small holdings scheme he gave certain figures. Here again I believe there are conditions which oould very well be discussed in a committee. I am not going to introduce individual cases here. I do not think this is the time for that, because it is late in the session, and when the committee is set up next year we can probably deal better with these matters.
However, there is one point in connection with veterans' reestablishment in regard to which I think something should be done before next session. That is the matter of grants to veterans who undertake cooperative farming. There has been one little difficulty in
this regard which I think should be ironed out. I refer to the case of a veteran who, after joining a cooperative, finds himself unable to agree with the others engaged in that undertaking, and wants to withdraw. I believe provision should be made whereby the land of the veteran will remain in the cooperative, because the whole business of that organization, the machinery and equipment the cooperative possesses, is acquired on the basis of the total land in the unit. If one member is allowed to withdraw his land another may do the same thing, and the result may be that the equipment will not be of the value it should be to the organization. I believe the minister is going to agree with me again.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I point out to
my hon. friend what we have already done in his own province in the matter of cooperatives? On February 19 of this year the provincial legislature passed the following resolution:
That this assembly, recognizing that veterans' land settlement is an urgent problem which, while primarily a federal responsibility, is nevertheless the concern of both federal and provincial authorities urge:
(1)	that the dominion and provincial governments give special assistance to communities in which veteran settlement of a pioneering nature is taking place;
(2)	that the government request the dominion government to bring in legislation to amend the Veterans Land Act to provide for:
(a)	The payment of grants to veterans' cooperative farming units in lieu of the V.L.A. credits of the veteran participants;
(b)	The purchase of land by V.L.A. for the purpose of establishing veterans cooperative farm units.
Similar proposals were considered by the House of Commons committee on veterans affairs, of which my hon. friend was a member, in 1946. That committee declined to agree to the principle embodied in paragraph 2(b) of the resolution passed by the legislature. In December, 1946, andi January, 1947, there were negotiations between Hon. J. H. Sturdy, minister of reconstruction, and rehabilitation of Saskatchewan, and the Department of Veterans Affairs. As a result, regulation 39 under the Veterans Land Act was adopted by order in council, permitting the director to advance up to $1,200 per veteran for the purchase of farm or forestry -equipment for the joint use of veterans cooperatively developing adjacent individual holdings under lease from the province, provided that the veteran had a right to purchase his holding and was not obligated to farm cooperatively.
The Hon. Mr. Sturdy, on behalf of the Saskatchewan government, signed an amendment to the agreement between the director
Supply-Veterans Affairs

and the Saskatchewan government giving effect to this regulation. Subsequently, further representations were made asking the dominion to make grants to cooperative farming organizations of veterans sponsored by the province.
On June 16 the director addressed the Saskatchewan convention of the Canadian Legion in Moose Jaw. He referred to the Saskatchewan government's proposals and said:
1.	The agreement between the dominion and provincial governments provides-
(a)	the province to make land available to
a veteran under 33-year lease with right to
purchase pr not to purchase.
(b)	the director to grant up to $2,326 in
chattels and equipment per veteran.
2.	Under this agreement 537 veterans have been established on provincial lands in Saskatchewan up to April 30, 1947.
3.	The province has made representations asking that the director make grants to cooperative farming societies whose by-laws provide that land chattels and labour be pooled and that if a member withdraws or is expelled he cannot withdraw his land.
4.	Such grants are not permissible under the Veterans Land Act, and consequently provision for them cannot be made in an agreement be-twees the two governments.
5.	Hence, if in the agreement between the province and an individual veteran there are provisions which conflict with the terms of the Veterans Land Act, the director could not legally make grants to such veterans.
I understand from my deputy minister that further applications came in yesterday from cooperative organizations in Saskatchewan and are being considered at the present time.

It was the last provision the minister has read in which I was particularly interested. I realize that the minister and his department have gone a long way in this matter. However, there is the final point where six, eight or ten men wish to form a cooperative and to get a grant of S2,520. The veteran is guaranteed that, upon his withdrawal from the cooperative, he will get out anything he has invested. It is considered that it is not fair that such a person should be able to withdraw his land, and it is urged that the land should remain in the cooperative. Otherwise, as I have said, this action completely breaks up the unit, and it becomes impossible to operate it in a cooperative manner because a particular piece of land may be one which is essential to the cooperative as a whole.
I would ask that the department give serious consideration to this. If it cannot be done under the act as it now stands, then I suggest that the act should be amended at another session of parliament. The department may not agree with what is being done in Saskat-

chewan; but we are part of Canada. We have decided we want to do things in a certain way; the veterans themselves have decided too, that they want to do things in a certain way. No veteran is being forced to go into cooperative farming, and it is only upon request that this type of unit is being set up. Where it is being set up at the request of veterans, and wdiere the people of Saskatchewan have decided they would like this particular way of farming and way of life, then, when there is a guarantee that the veteran will suffer no loss, I say the Department of Veterans Affairs should give consideration to meeting their request.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I can assure the hon. member that the department will review most carefully the entire situation.

The minister and his organization will remember the difficulty they had in Toronto back in 1943 and 1944 in connection with the handling of soldier patients. At that time some 12,000 subscribers had just completed a million dollar asset in the form of a hospital extension, which they were good enough to turn over to the Department of Veterans Affairs.
It has been the privilege of the subscribers who put up that million dollars to give service during the time when it was so badly needed when Sunnybrook was under construction. That time has now expired, and it is found necessary to evacuate the premises formerly occupied. One of the finest hospital buildings in Canada has been occupied by the patients of the department, numbering at times up to 240, and it has given service to the extent of over 100,000 patient-days a year. It not only gave hospital service, but there was added the service given by the community by serving four meals a day when only three were required, and other matters of that kind.
The entire community took a great interest in this work, and did w'hat we believe was a good job for the veterans who came back at that time from overseas. On July 1 those buildings were evacuated. The buildings have been subjected1 to four years of heavy wear and tear. On behalf of those 12,000 subscribers who put their private funds into that investment, I believe I need only mention that these buildings must be rehabilitated, and1 I feel sure the department will put them back into proper condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I interrupt the hon. member at that point? In the first place, the department is under a deep debt of gratitude to the hon. member, personally, for making available to us the facilities of

Supply-Veterans Affairs
the Toronto EJast General Hospital at a time when we needed hospital accommodation badly for our returning soldiers. Second, may I say to the hon. member that the condition of the hospital at the present time is being investigated by the Department of Public Works, and the proper conditioning will be done.

I have one other observation, and it is this. In the rush of getting equipment to service this building, certain equipment was received from the Department of Veterans Affairs. It is now subject to four years depreciation, and I would ask the minister to see to it that the department does not declare this equipment, of all kinds, as surplus, and turn it over to War Assets Corporation to be traded out or sold out. I suggest that he leave as much of it there as possible, in the economic interests of Canada, rather than advertise that partly used equipment as surplus.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at seven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: We are on item 454, departmental administration.

By leave of the committee, may I suggest that consideration be given to an honorarium for our present Deputy Chairman. He has worked very hard in hot weather for five or six weeks. I know he refused one before, but I should like to have this suggestion given consideration again.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I know you feel embarrassed. I am very grateful to the hon. member for Broadview for his suggestion. As a matter of fact an honorarium was suggested to the hon. member for Huron-Perth, but he declined. I think it could be done under the estimates for legislation if that is the committee's wish. I think that this time a measure of coercion and compulsion should be used which would be agreeable to all concerned.

I agree with the hon. member and the minister that our Chairman should be compelled by the house to accept what the house is so willing to grant. We never had a better chairman and if we could just keep him here all the time we would get through much sooner.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shall be very glad to take the matter up if that is the wish and will of the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I just associate this group with the suggestion that has been made, and thus make it unanimous.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Thank you very much. I shall be very glad indeed to see that the suggestion of the hon. member for Broadview is brought to the attention of the government when we reach the items under legislation.

Mr. Chairman, there are two or three questions I should like to place before the minister. This afternoon most of the su'b-. jects having to do with this department have been covered, and, I think, covered effectively, but I should like to have a statement from the minister with regard to these points. The first one has to do with a suggestion which was made by the Canadian Legion. Some weeks ago they presented a brief to the cabinet, and on July 7 they sent a copy of the brief to the members of the house, or possibly only to the members who served on the veterans committee last year. I think they have put their finger on one of the most important problems at the present time, and that is whether or not further consideration should be given to that group of Canadians who have suffered the most as a result of war service, or certainly have suffered as much as anybody else and perhaps more. The two groups to whom they refer are, first of all, pensioners who are so severely disabled that they are unable to do any work at all; second, the widows with young children to support who have no other means than the pension and family allowance.
These proposals were put forward to the committee last year, but it was more or less a new thought at the time and probably there was not as much consideration given as there should: have been. The legion are suggesting that the pensioner who is unable to1 work should be given a supplementary grant or pension of $25 a month provided that he is certified as unemployable by a competent medical authority.
With regard to the widows and children the legion asks that, while the children are growing and receiving an education, either the widow's pension be substantially increased or the children's allowances doubled. I believe that under the present rates the widow of a man who was killed overseas gets a pension of $60 a month, and if she has one child, an additional $15; for the second child, an additional $12, and. then $10 for each subsequent child. In addition to that she gets the family allowance. The legion suggests that during the period when the children are growing up and receiving their education the widow's pension should be at least at the present single man's
Supply-Veterans Affairs

100 per cent rate, $75 a month, if the rates payable for the children remain the same. In such a case a widow with one child would receive an annual pension and child's pension of $1,080. The other suggestion would be to double the children's allowance. There again the annual income would come to $1,080. These figures are where there is only one child.
That submission is made with a tremendous amount of public opinion behind it. The legion does not make recommendations of this type without having had them thought over carefully by their branches from coast to coast, and I think that, by and large, they represent public opinion on veterans affairs. I understand that the other soldier organizations which are also doing a splendid work agree with this submission. The suggestion is that something should be done without delay, that it should not be left over for another year. The brief concludes with these words:
We are also convinced that the tax-paying public of Canada, of which veterans form a very substantial part, will wish this obligation undertaken in behalf of those who have suffered most as a result of war services.
I can add nothing to that submission. Will the minister answer it?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, as far as I can. I am very grateful to my hon. friend for his constructive suggestions. I did have an interview with the Canadian Legion some time ago, and they also interviewed the Prime Minister and the cabinet with reference to the very points my hon. friend now raises. I received notice that my hon. friend was going to ask a question with reference to preenlistment condition not aggravated during service.
That question is coming later.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend asked with reference to those pensioners who are unable to work. We are doing a lot of constructive work now under Eddie Dunlop, a blinded ex-service man himself, who, as my hon. friend, who is a front line soldier himself, knows, is in charge of the casualty and rehabilitation section and is placing many of the heavily disabled men in employment.
These men to whom the legion refers are pensioners who are certified by a doctor to be unable to work.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes. Of course that is a special case, different from what I had in mind. I was talking of the mem who are seriously handicapped and1 who can get placement in employment.
The next question had to do with widows of men who were overseas, with young

children to support. I think there is a terribly strong moral appeal, and also a national appeal on their behalf, and I can assure my hon. friend that we shall give, it-I do not like the word "consideration" because I think there is a parliamentary falsification to it-anxious attention and assiduous care, as much as we can and as soon as we can.
Is there something that can be done before next session? There can be no legislation now for perhaps nine or ten months.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As I understand' the difficulties, it affects the whole basic pension scheme and may require legislation at the next session of parliament, but we shall look into it most carefully and sympathetically and see if anything can be effected by regulation, because I know my colleagues are sympathetic to the last point mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver South. Whether we can do it by regulation I am not sure, but in any event it will not be forgotten but will be carefully remembered.

The second question has to do with war veterans allowances. There is a principle that must be settled with regard to war veterans allowance, and I think it is this, whether or not the government accepts full responsibility for the recipients of that allowance. Mention was made earlier in the day of the fact that the position is now such that in some of the provinces war veterans allowance recipient cannot get as much as the old age pensioner. In Ontario they get $9.59 a month less. In British Columbia there is the difference between $30.41 and $38.75, and there is a difference in several other of the provinces. Personally I have always understood that the veteran getting war veterans allowance is solely the charge of the dominion government. We are entitled to know whether or not the government is still acknowledging that responsibility because, if it is, there can be no doubt that war veterans allowance recipients should be put in the same position as the old age pensioner. The allowance was originally intended to be an old age pension for the veterans. It was made payable at age sixty on the basis that he had become preaged because of his service. It is now in a most unfortunate position, because I can assure the minister that- in our own city of Vancouver there are many of these war veteran allowances recipients who are not able to exist on the present allowance. Here again the time element is of the utmost importance.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I say at once to my hon. friend that there is no question whatsoever-

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I also include the widows who come under the War Veterans Allowances Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They have been fairly well treated in the last two years as a result of the advocacy of the hon. member for Davenport. I think the vote is $2,100,000 this year for widows and children, which can help quite a lot; whereas they were not getting a single cent two or three years ago. That is what this parliament did for them. I think that is a real improvement. In regard to the general basic rates for veterans allowances, I agree at once with my hon. friend that it is entirely a federal responsibility; it was a federal act when enacted in 1930. The improvements were all made by the various federal parliaments and federal governments from that time until now. What the ultimate plan may be with reference to approximate equalization with old age pension rates I am not in a position to say. It is a matter of government policy to be decided but I can at least assure my hon. friend that the question will receive the most careful attention of the administration as soon as possible.
The dominion government is accepting full responsibility?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It always did.
For the war veterans allowance recipients?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It always did.
And still is?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Certainly.

A word with regard to the pension payable to merchant seamen. I hold in my hand the last edition of Veterans Affairs. This is a semi-monthly publication got out by the minister's department and an interesting publication it is. This issue is dated July 15, 1947. I find practically half of the front page taken up with an article entitled "Schooner Thought U-boat Victim". It describes an appeal to the appeal board of the Canadian pension commission against the adverse decision made by the pension commission in the case of a Canadian who was on a Newfoundland schooner which was lost en route from Newfoundland to a point, I think, in the West Indies. His widow's claim for a pension was disallowed on the ground that it had not been shown that the death of her husband was directly attributable to enemy action. This case shows more clearly than any argument a member could make on the floor of the house that the present law with regard to paying pension to the dependents 83166-368
of a merchant seaman who lost his life or to a merchant seaman -who was disabled is far, far too strict. First of all, it requires that the injury must have arisen from the direct result of enemy action. The second thing is that there is a time limit of one year for the application to be made. I will just ask the minister to read his own magazine, and when he reads that story I am quite sure he will be convinced that there must be an amendment made to the act. I think it is called the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. I will not go into the matter any further this evening, but the whole story is in the minister's own paper. I hope that there will be no further opposition from the government to having that act amended.
Another group whose position should be further considered are the men who flew transports across the Atlantic. They do not get the benefits recommended last year by the committee. I believe it has now been clearly established that they were treated by the British government as though they had been in the forces and that they were given medals for their service. I would ask the minister to give us the assurance that their case will be placed before the committee when it sits next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Certainlj'.

Finally, I should like to refer to the ruling that men are not entitled to pension because they had a pre-enlistment condition. When the committee sat last year we were given figures made up by the Canadian pension commission, which showed that up to December 31, 1945, there had been 7,810 men refused entitlement on the ground that they had a pre-enlistment condition which was not aggravated by service. That number comprised men who actually got abroad. They had gone to Great Britain or some other theatre of war, subsequently were discharged as unfit, and yet it w'as held that because they had a pre-enlikbment condition they were not entitled to pension. The same statement gave ithe figure of 54.207 for men who had service only in Canada. They had enlisted as fit, served in Canada and were discharged as unfit, and yet W'ere ruled ineligible for pension because it was found that they had a pre-enlistment condition. That made a total of about 62,000.
Tonight I am not going into the fight we had last year over the question, but I still think the government was wrong in refusing to make a change and write a presumption into the Pension Act. I should like to get the figures from December 31, 1945, until the present time. I wish to know the additional
