numbers who have been ruled against on the ground of a pre-enlistment condition, divided into those who served overeeas and those who had service only in Canada, so 'that the figures given to me tonight can be added to the figures given to us by the pension commission last year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The pension commission were so taxed in giving effect to the various amendments put through, and in the new applications they had to deal with, that 'they have not those figures available, but they will be obtained as soon as possible and given to the hon. member. Of course this is also a matter that will be of interest to the committee when it is set up next year.
Have I to wait until next year for the figures?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No. They will be obtained and given as soon as we can get them from the records division.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for Fort William for permitting me a minute at this .time. I wish to raise this matter now in support of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver South. It relates to veterans allowances. I can save time and make my own point clear by reading a brief extract from the letter of a world war I veteran that has been on my file for some time. If I read it the position will be clear. It supports the position which the hon. member for Vancouver South 'took and which those on this side took in this morning's debate. It states:
I am calling to ask you to try and clear up a somewhat ambiguous situation which has arisen out of the recent amending of the old age pension provisions. A war veteran who is in receipt of veterans allowance is placed on the Indian list as far as old age pension is concerned. That veteran cannot qualify for old age pension benefits. His veterans allowance is at present $30 a month. If nothing is now done we will have an unjust discrimination as between the ordinary pensioner and the aged veteran, particularly in Ontario. There before another year rolls around we will have the ordinary pensioner with a monthly income of $40 and the aged veteran with an income of $30 a month. Surely if there is to be a difference the veteran should be the favoured one.
He goes on to refer to a statement supposed to have been made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs, that the government did not intend to open up this veterans legislation this year. He says that if this is not done the Old Age Pensions Act should be amended so that the veterans should be assisted and not be at a disadvantage.
I present that letter to emphasize the point taken by the hon. member for Vancouver
[Mr. Given.1
South. My understanding is that the minister says he is unable at this time to give a positive statement that any greater financial aid can be given, but that he is saying that the matter will receive consideration after prorogation.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. I wish to thank my hon. friend for his constructive suggestion. The difficulty is that the federal authority is not aware of what the various provinces will do by way of supplementing whatever grant is made in the form of old age pension, and by January next, when I hope we meet again, the situation will have become stabilized and we shall be able then to assess the contributions made jointly in regard to old age pensions by the dominion and the provinces and to meet the point raised in the communication the hon. member has read.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have one observation to make with respect to that. The minister himself said that this matter of war veterans allowances was entirely a matter of federal responsibility. I trust that, whatever action is taken or not taken by the provinces with respect to old age pensions, it will have no bearing on the question of the dominion government dealing justly with the war veterans.
Mr. MclVOR: In the last few years I have had considerable trouble with veterans of the first war, and I speak now to give a little bit of advice to those who have been in the same position that I have been in. I have had case after case straightened out and those old veterans will agree that my plan was sound. My plan was to write to the deputy minister or especially to Brigadier-General Melville, chairman of the pension commission, and give him the particulars. Do that and you will get a reply by return mail. Not long ago an old veteran gave me language plainer than polite. I have had cases straightened- out in a very satisfactory manner, and I would say to hon. members that what is even better than making speeches in the House of Commons is to get in touch with the chairman of the pension commission.

I wish to ask
the Minister of Veterans Affairs if he would consult the appropriate member of the cabinet-I imagine it is the Minister of Finance-and also the wartime prices and trade board with respect to houses which have been bought by veterans, which were tenanted, and possession of which they could not obtain. Those who bought houses before July 26, 1945, are able to apply for possession of them; but the other fellows who were late in coming back, later than those who

Supply-Veterans Affairs
could take advantage of that provision, find themselves in the position I have indicated. Some of them perhaps did not understand the regulations, but for one reason or another they bought these houses. I have received many letters and am going to read extracts from a couple of them to show what it is all about. I quote from one:
Why are young Canadians disgusted? Why do they want to go to the U.S.A.? Here are some of my reasons:	Housing restrictions-veteran's family, seriously disrupted by six years separation while in the service, frozen out of a tenant-occupied home. This same tenant sat quietly on civvy street during the war and still is-while my family, and hundreds like us- still scratching for inadequate accommodation. The one feature was aggravated reestablishment more than any other.
That is just one letter. I will read part of another:
. . . my husband had joined the R.C.A.F. immediately at the outbreak of war. Our home was broken up for six years, as I followed him in Canada.
After buying a tenant-occupied home because the tenants told the agent he wanted him to find them a house to move into, we find they immediately changed their mind and informed us they will not buy for several years when prices are reduced.
Those are only two examples of many letters I have received. I spoke over the radio on July 1, asking the young men and women not to go to the United States. These letters are in reply to that appeal. They all give the same reasons. The veterans cannot get the houses which they have bought. It seems to me that they deserve some attention and that regulations should be made in order that they might be able to get possession of the houses for which they have paid good money. I would ask the minister if he would not use his good auspices with the proper authorities with a view to having the regulations changed so that these people will be able to get their houses.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I wish to assure the
hon. member for St. Paul's that the weighty assignment which he has placed upon my shoulders will be discharged by the officers of the department as far as possible. We have already made representations in the direction he has indicated.

Mr. Chairman, I want to have some information about what is done by the department, and the question is not merely regarding the spending of money. It is as to what is done with the money which is spent. It is a simple thing I want to know.
I was told today-and it was a surprise to ' me-that members of parliament insisted on having veterans affairs estimates brought down earlier than the others; there were 83166-368*
some answers for that. But I remember distinctly that when the estimates of the department were brought in for the first time, they were just like a flying cloud. When I rose to ask a question-this is about a month ago; I have not looked up the record, but my recollection is clear about it-I was immediately told that there was nothing before the chair. It had all gone away-phut!-like that. I have waited for a month now, and tonight I want to get some information.
In the first place, my idea is that all the money which is spent for veterans is well spent, provided that it is spent on men who have been in the Canadian army. But that is not what is done. My fear is that most of the grants of the Department of Veterans Affairs are expended in another branch of the immigration business, and that veterans who never belonged to the Canadian army-veterans of the imperial army or some other one, or erven of the home guards-are brought in and given the advantages of the legislation which has been passed to help Canadians or members of the Canadian army. I remember having seen in the press something about the visit of the minister to the estate of the Duke of Sutherland or someone else in England or Scotland; it was somewhere in the British isles. Afterwards we were told by the press that, as a result of the visit, 30,000 men of the imperial army would come to Canada as immigrants.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, oh.

I do not want the minister to laugh, because I am serious; and when I am serious, I mean it. I want him to be polite. I gave him a lesson today and1 I did not use all of my repertoire which is parlia^ mentary. But I want the minister to be polite, if not for the last time, at least for the first time this session. I mean what I say.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: So do I.

The minister means
nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member means less to me.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

Now, there is progress for you. We understand what the minister has said. As a rule, I cannot understand what he saiys and that is the reason why I object to it. When he mumbled an answer of some kind and I asked the Minister of Labour and the then secretary of state what the Minister of Veterans Affairs had said, they told me they could not understand him, and they were quite close to him. The minister can say anything to me; provided that he
Supply-Veterans Affairs

speaks intelligibly I Shall be satisfied. But I want him to speak the English language correctly. That is all I want him to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I speak it better than the hon. member does.
Certainly. It is the minister's own language. He took honours in college, and it would be shameful if he could not speak his own language better than I can.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not my own language.
It is the language of those Who burned the house of his great grandmother.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Let us rise and report progress.

That being said, it is only a preliminary. I want to get some information with regard to the mysteries of the Department of Veterans Affairs. Members are easy to satisfy. They hear a grunt of some kind and they say, "He is so clever; he is a nice fellow. I am satisfied." I shall not be satisfied with a grunt. I want more than that. I want an explanation and I want figures. I am not referring to figures of money but rather to figures of results. I want to know how the money has been spent. I want to know whether those who have taken advantage of this legislation are Canadians or blokes. The question is a simple one. When I use the word "blokes" I do not mean those who were bom outside of Canada. I mean those who are migratory birds, those who come here just to take advantage of the money which is voted for Canadian purposes. That includes people who were born in any part of the world, but who have come to Canada to settle down and make in Canada a home for themselves, their children and grandchildren. I do not want to be misjudged or misunderstood. I want to be clearly understood. I want to know what has been done with the money which has been voted and which runs up into such high figures. I want to know how many people have been benefited by each one of the acts which were passed last session. I want to know how many people who were in the Canadian army have received advantages and benefits from any of those acts. I want to know how many others, non-Canadians, have benefited from each one of those acts. To save the time of the committee I will mention the chapters of the statutes of 1946. They are chapters 36, 43, 52, 59, 62, 63. 66, 69, 70, 71, 72, 74 and 75. It is just a question I was asking the first time the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs were brought in; and after I rose to my

feet I had only time to begin to ask my question before I was told there was nothing before the Chair. It was gone-phut!-just like that. I want that information now, please.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Right away sir; it is all here. All beneficiaries were Canadians born or domiciled in this country prior to service in the imperial or allied forces. The beneficiaries under each act have been classified as having served (a) in Canadian forces; (b) in British forces; (c) in allied forces. Pensions, world war I: Canadians, 87,318; others, British domiciled in Canada, 250; allied, 34, or a total of non-Canadians of 284 as against a complete Canadian total of 87,318. World war II: Canadians, 87,558; others, British, 135; allied 3, or a total of 138 as against an all-Canadian total of 87,558.
War veterans allowance: Canadians, 25,112; others, British, 916; allied, 215, or a total of 1,131 as against an all-Canadian total of 25,112.
Veterans Land Act: Canadian and British, 25 188; allied, 36. The number of British were estimated at 100 to 150, and the details are not exactly available in regard to that total.
Out of work allowances, under the legislation passed by this parliament: Canadians, 156,912; others, British, 65; allied, 40, or a total of 105 as against an all-Canadian total of 156,912.
Vocational training:	Canadian, 85,848;
o.thers, British 42; allied, 36, or a total of 78 as against an all-Canadian total of 85,848.
Awaiting benefit returns: Canadians, 43,227; others, British, 5; allied, 24, or a total of 29 as against an all-Canadian total of 43,227.
Temporary incapacity, one of the special benefits this parliament has arranged: Canadians, 5,178; others, British, 0; allied. 0; as against a grand Canadian total of 5,178.
University training for our young men: Canadians, 54,968; others, British, 44; allied, 37, or a total of 81 as against an all-Canadian total of 54,968.
Gratuities-and this is perhaps the most crushing reply given by these figures to the suggestion that has been adduced so unfairly in this house: Canadians, 941.311; others. British, 3,285; allied, 403, or a total of 3,688 as against a Canadian total of 941,311.
Reestablishment credits, and the only country in the world to have done this is our country of Canada: Canadians, 650,000; others, British 129; allied, 232, or a total of 361 as against a Canadian total of 650,000.
Business and professional loans, which are under the jurisdiction of my colleague the Minister of Finance: Canadians, 2,024; others,

Supply-Veterans Affairs
British, 4; allied, 3, or a total of 7 as against a Canadian total of 2,024.
The Veterans Insurance Act: Canadians, 11,222; others, British 25; allied, 0, or 25 as against a Canadian total of 11,222. The few British I have mentioned as entitled to these various benefits were Canadians who served in the Royal Air Force and saved England and freedom in the battle of Britain.
I wonder if the minister made these calculations himself. Did he personally check the records of these thousands of people?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The calculation was made under my direction by trusted and worthy officers of the department.

Yes, but the minister
knows no more about the matter than I do. They were prepared by his staff, but he has never checked them. What surprises me is that the figures run to even thousands. It is not a case of odd numbers at all; it is 500, 1,000 and so many thousands.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

Except for the last figures. The large ones are all that way; they are even 500's or even 1,000's. But now I want the minister to understand my point of view, and I am sure he will relish it. It will not take me long to explain it. He said that men who belonged to the British army were defending liberty throughout the world. That is true, but my point of view is that the men who served in the British army ought to be paid pensions by the British government. We are looking after our own people; why should we pay pensions to men who served in another army?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: These are all Canadians, every one of them.

That is all right, but they are Canadians who were not in the Canadian army but in another army. The minister knows very well the number of those who served in the imperial army and who now want to take advantage of the Canadian pension scheme in order to get more money. Some of them are men Who have never been in Canada but who want to come here as one wants to go to a garden of Eden, to a promised land.
This whole matter should also be considered from another angle, in regard to those who signed for overseas service and those who did not. This is the military preference as established by the Department of Veterans Affairs and the old Department of Pensions
and National Health. It is to the effect that a man who was in the home guard in England, a man who was always near the gate of his garden all the time, was entitled to an overseas preference over a Canadian who had been in the Canadian army, who had followed the instructions of his superior officers, who had been to Kiska, who had been to Labrador, but who had not signed for overseas. The gallantry of a man was not to fight in battle, was not to isolate himself from his family, to suffer the cold or heat of distant parts of the hemisphere; it was to sign for overseas. I know men who suffered from paralysis, who suffered from double rupture, who suffered from heart conditions and who were completely unfit, but who signed for overseas service in the expectation of having a discharge. But at the same time they were given a button to show itheir gallantry when they signed enlistment papers for overseas. They were gallant, they were courageous because of the stroke of a pen.
The others were not given the same advantages as the former ones because they had not signed for overseas. At the present time there are a large number of soldiers who have done their duty and who have obeyed the orders they have received from their superior officers, but who have been guilty of the crime of not signing the form to serve overseas. It was a great crime which deprived them of the preference and even of the benefits of certain legislation.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister, so that in the millennium some change will be made in the absurd provisions of the Civil Service Act. I am not in a hurry for my answer; I shall be satisfied if it is tabled at. the beginning of the next session. But I would ask the minister to table a list of the individual names of the men included in each of the totals he gave not long ago. I want to know the true addresses of each of those men included among those thousands of men mentioned not long ago and, as I say, I shall be satisfied to have that information at the beginning of the next session. Now that the calculation is made, it will be easy to give that list, because if the work of the Department of Veterans Affairs has been well done the list is now ready; and that list will have been made in several copies so that it will be easy to table one copy at the next session.
I say to the minister that I always act in a friendly spirit and in a friendly disposition. I am not impressed by high position or high-sounding titles. That means nothing to me, because I am a democrat. I do not see what
Supply-Veterans Affairs

advantage it is for Canada to have minister who is a member of the privy council at Westminster. It means only that he is an English minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: More like a Scotch minister, I should say.

But I take that view, the Canadian view. I am not impressed by the fact of his being a privy councillor. One cannot serve two countries; one cannot serve England and Canada at the same time. If one is created a right honourable he might be tempted to serve England first, before Canada, and my idea is that Canada should be served first. However, that is only a matter of opinion.
I will tell the minister what, among other things, is wrong in the Department of Veterans Affairs. I do not wish to be unfair to anyone in that department. The fault is that when a decision is made it is impossible to have it reconsidered favourably. I have in mind particularly the case of a cousin of mine who served in North Africa for several years. He was there, and in that country there were tarantulas and snakes; indeed, it was like some departments in that respect. They did not have a very pleasant life over there. My cousin was there for a long time, and he had some trouble with a bureaucrat in Quebec city who went to England just for a Cook's tour. I now make a comparison between a man who served in the air force and who wanted to take advantage of legislation which would make his life more pleasant and which would improve his condition-a real soldier-on the one hand, and on the other hand a bureaucrat who went to England for two months at the end of the war and thereby qualified himself for overseas service. I find that pretty hard to digest. I have asked questions about that man; I shall not name him tonight. But I want him to bend before the authority, and that authority I would name as the superior officer in the department. I want justice for the man I first mentioned.
Some people are under the impression that because a man has been wearing a uniform he is a full-fledged soldier. I am not. I have never been in the army, and I am too old now to serve in it, but I have served, the soldiers. I have been a servant of the people and of the returned men. I have petitions right here in Ottawa. There is a Victoria Cross winner right here in th'e building, and I looked after him. And when another Victoria Cross winner from British Columbia was in trouble he sent me an S.O.S. down the river. I must give credit

to the minister for having fixed him up. Nevertheless it was a great honour for me to receive word from that gentleman who was a distinguished soldier from British Columbia and brought glory to Canada in the first war.
That man was completely abandoned. However I am not going to tell the story, because it is known to hon. members. But what I have said indicates that I am sincere when I say I look after those men. I do it for their own good and for the country's good. I do not want any fascism in this country; I do not want any communism; I do not want any subversive ideas. I want order and authority.
I will tell you, Mr. Chairman, and the minister, that if the men are not fairly dealt with, anything can be expected from them. I say that in all honesty; and I want the minister to understand well that when representations are made to him or to his most intelligent and capable parliamentary assistant, or to the deputy minister, or to the head of the pension commission, we should have some satisfactory replies.
Since this is either the last day or the day preceding the close of the session, I shall not insist any further in what I am saying. But I tell the minister again that in the future he has to be polite, and he must understand that while he is a right honourable he is still the servant of the people, just the same as are other members in the house.

Despite anything that may have been said in debate, I feel that in many respects the minister has done a good job in the Department of Veterans Affairs. If he has not done a better job it is probably due to pressure from the treasury board. However, the government in that regard will have to accept the responsibility for anything that has not been done in the Department of Veterans Affairs.
I hope what I have to say next will not prove contentious. I feel that at this time the government should give consideration to the arranging of an excursion at substantially reduced rates to the battlefields of Europe for the next, of kin of Canadian boys who are buried there. Such an excursion at reduced rates should be planned for not later than 1948, when I believe shipping ought to be available.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to deal with this item.

I would ask the minister if there is any other item on which I could bring this up. I shall 'take only a moment or two. I believe that this opportunity to visit the graveyards of Canada's sons who are buried

Supply-Veterans Affairs
on 'foreign soil should be granted to the next of kin, most of whom I feel are financially unable to make 'the trip. Such an excursion under the sponsorship of the government would be a fine gesture on the part of a grateful country toward these families who have sacrificed so much for Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I do not see how the hon. member can relate his proposal to the 'Department of Veterans Affairs.
Where else can I bring it up, Mr. Chairman, if not here? I think it should be under the veterans affairs department.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
When the Vimy pilgrimage in 1936 was arranged the present deputy minister was chairman of the committee and I was minister of national defence in charge of arrangements. Personally, Mr. Chairman, with your consent and the consent of the committee, perhaps the hon. gentleman might be allowed to speak briefly.
Mr. MoKAY: I consider it the duty of the government to those who have lost their sons or husbands or fathers overseas to do everything possible to see that 'they have at least one opportunity to visit the graves of their loved ones who lie over 'there. That is all I have to say upon that subject, Mr. Chairman.
I now wish to associate myself with 'those who have spoken 'this afternoon and (this evening urging the minister to give serious consideration to raising the basic pension, not only for the disability pensioners, but for recipients of 'the veteran's allowance and the widow's allowance. We all know that the cost of living has gone up and is continuing to rise. We also know that the United States has increased its pensions by 20 per cent. I have been informed that the cost of living in the United States has gone up so much that the veterans pensions were inadequate. I do not for one moment suggest that Canada up to now has not done as well as the United States with regard to pensions. Canada has done a good job, but the rising cost of living makes it very difficult for our pensioners ito carry on. It is ridiculous to suggest that anyone can live on $30.41, which is the amount which the war veteran receives under the War Veterans Allowances Act. The widow of a deceased veteran who receives only $60 a month is receiving altogether too small an amount. If she has two children she receives an additional $27. That does not go very far these days in providing shelter, food, clothing and medical care. So I appeal to the minister to do everything he can to see that the basic pensions for these groups are raised and raised without delay.

The minister will recall that last year a number of us accompanied him to the veterans health and occupational centre at Billings Bridge and were favourably impressed with the lay-out, recreation facilities, treatment, meals and accommodation. This session a couple of the veterans from there came to see me. They reminded me that the minister, when down there, had told them that if there were any complaints they should let him know. They said they did not like to bother him and asked me to take their case up. I took it up with the department and it was straightened out satisfactorily. Last night one of them said that twelve others would like me to take their cases up. I said I did not think that was the right channel. I would suggest to the minister, if he will accept my suggestion, that he send one of his deputy ministers to Billings Bridge to see these, men, investigate their complaints and try to get to the bottom of the trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That will be done right away.

I can give the minister the name of the man to get in touch with. There is one clause in the Pension Act which should be given consideration. It is with regard to pre-enlistment disability. The way that is interpreted by the board is this. Suppose a man comes up during the war or following the war for duodenal ulcer. His history was taken overseas in hospital, and the attending doctor takes the case history something like this:	"Have you
ever had stomach trouble before?" "No." "Just think it over." "Well, I did have stomach trouble ten years ago, but I got some treatment for two or three weeks and it all cleared up." Then down on his history sheet goes the item; "Stomach trouble, 1935." He comes up for pension for duodenal ulcer, and the pension is refused because of that item on his history sheet. The pension board say, "We cannot do anything for you. You had stomach trouble in 1935. Pre-enlistment disability." So he is only pensionable for aggravation. I assure the minister that the;e are plenty of these cases happening
Supply-Veterans Affairs

where the pension, is refused on just as flimsy a thing as that, where the soldier overseas, with no thought of concealment wilfully or otherwise, foolishly gave one of these details which went down on his history sheet. If this debate goes on here for two or three days more everybody in this house will have nervous indigestion, but that should not preclude us from being pensioned for duodenal ulcer. I assure the minister that I have many cases where the ruling made by the pension board is pinned on just as flimsy a pretext as that. The history may show a duodenal ulcer ten years ago. There is no reason why the pension board should claim that that is a perfect history. It was not confirmed by X-ray; there was no confirmation, no diagnosis made at that time. Unless such diagnosis is confirmed, either by X-ray or doctor's certificate or by admission, the applicant should not be refused a pension. Therefore I claim that this clause is being badly interpreted by the board. I assure the minister that I am absolutely honest in this matter. There has been no attempt by me to obtain pensions under that ruling. To be honest about this matter, I assured myself that these cases were being unjustly dealt with. The presentation of these cases before the house gains nothing whatever. Very few of them are couched in language we can understand, and it is difficult to decide just what should be done when they are presented before the house.
I was interested this afternoon in the presentation of cases by several hon. members, but I could not form any opinion, and I have been over the files of some of these cases. I came to the conclusion that we are dealing with psychoneurosis, which brings me to another clause which, I think, should have freer interpretation than is given at the present time. A man with psychoneurosis, provided that it is due to battle fatigue or whatever it may be

and much has been written about it at this time-suffers the tortures of the damned, possibly worse than a man who has a combat injury. Yet it is a difficult matter to interpret, and is very difficult for the pension board. I will make an appeal to the minister and to the pension board. I think the part dealing with psychoneurosis should not be just cast aside, and say that he is just a neurotic. A person who is suffering from psychoneurosis is undergoing a worse disability than a person who has lost a leg or two legs. I ask the pension board to deal kindly with these cases, to look into them, and if there is any suspicion that it is due to war service the individual concerned should be given the full benefit of the doubt.

I leave that other matter for the consideration of the committee, because I realize that we discussed it for two days in. the pension committee. I do not blame the pension board, because we created that act and wrote in that clause, but I feel that many applicants for pension are not receiving a fair deal under that clause and that we should rewrite it. It should be broadened and there should be a clear way of interpreting it in order to assist the pension board. They cannot do anything with it at the present time, because they turn up the history of these cases. Every one of us has suffered disabilities or sickness. You can get hundreds of histories from any one of us if you tried. We should be very careful in interpreting that and not pick up something for which there is no proof whatever. A war disability should be proved by X-ray, a definite statement of a doctor, or an admission from the applicant himself.

Once again I should like to renew a plea which has been made every year since I have been here, in behalf of the imperial veterans, those men who served in the first world war from 1914 to 1918, who came to Canada and have lived as Canadian citizens ever since, making their full contribution to the life of this country. I am not going to spea'k at length on this matter, but I want to sajr this. I have not previously expressed myself on the matter of the many increases in salary which have lately been granted, but it seems to me that if we can grant pensions of $3,000 to diplomats after five years of service; if we can increase the salaries of the leaders in the other place, we can at last afford to pay the war veterans allowances to these old and comparatively few veterans who, in the first war, served alongside our own soldiers. Many of the benefits given under the veterans charter of Canada are generous, but I feel that the continued denial of this small concession to these men under the circumstances is narrow-minded and mean, and I renew the plea to the minister to extend the war veterans allowances to imperial veterans who have been in Canada for a specified number of years.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I find no fault whatever with the advocacy of the hon. member for Kamloops. I have frequently stated my personal policy on this matter, but perhaps the committee will pardon me if I restate it in the space of about one minute. This matter came up before the veterans affairs committee last year, and the stand I took at that time was endorsed by that committee. Very simply my stand was this. Before we extend the war veterans allowances to imperials-and I was born over there-we should give it to all Canadians who served in England, in Canada or in a theatre of actual war. That should be done before we extend the allowance'to any imperial, even though he may have been domiciled here before July, 1930, which is the advocacy that has been made on their behalf. I have nothing but the greatest admiration for those gallant imperial soldiers, but I am a Canadian through and through. Many of our men could not get overseas through no fault of their. own, but they served in khaki, they served in the forces; and I say it is wrong to give the veteran's allowances to imperials before you give it to every single Canadian who served in the forces.
Then why not give it to all those Canadians?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We certainly are not doing it.
I say, do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will support my hon. friend in that as far as I can, but that is the policy I have been trying to advocate with the government. I have made no secret of it; I have mentioned it everywhere, on every platform.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let us go the whole way and pay a pension to everyone.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think it might be a fine scheme of social security to give it to those who served in Canada, those who served in England and those who served in any theatre of actual war, and also to the imperial veterans. But it would not be the war veteran's allowance any longer; it would be a part of the great social security system in Canada.

I should like to ask the minister a question in regard to the pensions advocates. Will he explain the information at page 261 of the estimates which places the pensions advocates at various grades. First, will he explain the way in which they are graded as grades 1, 2, 3 and 4. I bake it that these pensions advocates are members of the bar and are devoting their full time to this job, with the exception, of course, of those who are operating part time. If these rates of pay are correct I say they are totally inadequate for the service these men are rendering. I would suggest that pensions advocates should be the best counsel procurable and should be paid salaries in accordance with the service they render. How many cases do pensions advocates handle in a year, and what success have they had with those oases?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to say one further brief but earnest word on this item, in addition to what I said this morning. Before doing so, however, may I join sincerely in the compliments which others have been paying the minister upon the way in which he handles the cases which members take up with him. Now that there are so few ministers in the house, so that what I shall say will not embarrass them, I believe I express the view
Supply-Veterans Affairs

of members generally when I say that the Minister of Veterans Affairs is the best minister in the cabinet, so far as dealing with correspondence is concerned. Any faults we find with him relate, not to the way in which he administers the legislation which comes within his purview, but rather to the scope of that legislation. In many instances we feel it should be widened.
This is one instance where earnest and, I hope, favourable consideration may be given at the earliest possible moment. This item concerns the special allowances paid to widows of non-pensioned veterans. Earlier this evening when we were discussing the general item replying to the hon. member for Vancouver South the minister said that this provision had been in existence for only eighteen months. He was not quite fair to himself when he said that. Actually it has been in existence for four years. Back in 1943 an allowance of S25 a month was brought in by the minister, and in 1944 it was increased to the present figure of $30.41 a month. Last year it was transferred from an annual item in the estimates to the War Veterans Allowances Act itself. I am sure that the minister recognizes the force of the argument which was made this morning and which is being made now, that with the old age pension up in many provinces to $35 or $40 a month it is not fair to ask these non-pensioned veterans' widows to live on $30.41 a month. They have been, in my view, most reasonable in the requests which they have made repeatedly to the government that the amount should be raised to $40. I think they would be well advised to be pressing for $50, but at least I hope the minister will soon find a way of increasing the present amount to one or other of these figures.
At the same time I hope that consideration will be given to some of the other requests which the organization representing these women has made. In particular, they have asked that this provision be extended to widows of veterans who, in the first great war, saw service only in England and did not get to the continent. They go farther knd would like to have it extended to widows of all non-pensioned veterans of the first world war. I -urge that steps in the right direction be taken in connection with this matter.
I also urge on the minister the requests of these women for consideration in the matter of hospitalization. They do not ask, as the minister, I think, misunderstood last year, to be hospitalized in the veterans hospitals, but they do ask for financial consideration in connection with their hospital needs.
This appeal on behalf of these widows is a request with which there is complete sym-

pathy in all quarters of the house. The minister earlier this evening assured the hon. member for Vancouver South that the whole question of the War Veterans Allowances Act-would be given consideration. These women are now included in that act; I hope that the minister can give us an assurance that he will do his best to have this amount increased, and when he has done so he will get still more compliments from all sides of the house. I am glad to see him nodding his head.

I associate myself with the remarks just now made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and I want especially to thank the minister again for his continued support in connection with this item from the very beginning. I believe I was the first or one of the first to bring this question up in the house years ago, and from the very beginning the minister was * sympathetic. In the last two or three years when we were pressing to have the amount increased, again he was sympathetic, until now it is up to $30.41 a month. With the old age pensions act in Ontario now calling for $40 a month, I hope that the minister will consider advancing the pension of these widows to at least as much as the old age pension in Ontario, $40 a month. I also wish to associate myself in supporting the other requests urged upon the minister by the hon. member.

These widows are all getting older and they cannot work as they used to be able to work. The widow of a man with a pension of less than fifty per cent who dies of a pensionable disability receives the full amount of the pension but if he dies from: a non-pensionable cause two weeks before he might have died from a pensionable disability she gets only $30 a month. I have always thought this circumstance was so very unfair. The minister has spoken in support of raising the amount which these widows will get. I hope it will not be long before they get an increased amount, because the cost of living is going up and they are all getting older.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Will the minister make
a comment?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The only comment
I could make is that I am deeply impressed' by the kindly remarks of my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre, by the genial cooperation of my hon. friend the member for Davenport and by the concurrence of my hon. friend the memb.er for St. Paul's.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
But what about thewidows?

Supply-Veterans Affairs

I wish to join my
voice with those who have been advocating a fairer deal for the widows of veterans of world war I. Our treatment of them has been very shabby and constitutes a reflection on our nation as a whole. If there is anyone who is handicapped in making a living it is a widow and especially the widow of a war veteran.
I have a case which I think is worthy of consideration which has been brought to my attention. It is that of the widow of Archibald N. Forrest, 2043157, 74th Battery. He enlisted in 1916, was struck off strength in 1921. This man was hurt at Petawawa and spent six weeks in Sydenham hospital. His case was heard before the pension commission and they offered him an operation for double hernia. He asked if he might have his own doctor but was refused that privilege. He then refused to undergo the operation, because the doctors in charge would not promise him that he would be any better after the operation than before. Apparently, as a consequence of his having refused that operation, they changed his category from C-3 to A-l, according to the information given to me. How any doctor would be justified in doing a thing of that sort, I cannot understand. It made all the difference between this man being eligible for some sort of pension and not being eligible, 'because changing his category passed him as physically fit, though actually he was suffering from double hernia.
He did not try for pension again until June or July, 1937, when he filed his application through the Army and Navy Veterans. He was awaiting a medical board when he died in October. His widow has had a very difficult time and is still having an extremely difficult time, living right here in Ottawa almost in the shadow of this building. She went before the pension commission and got nothing. She tried to get into the civil service, but was told that she was too old to get in, being over thirty-five years of age. Then she set about to try to have the age limit for widows entering the civil service raised, and I understand that she had some measure of success and finally got into the service. She worked there during the war and her hekl'th broke down. She is now forty-nine years old and is unable to get any work and unable to get a pension. There she is. How we can expect a woman of that kind to live is a question to which I believe all members of the government should devote some attention. I just mention this as one case. There .are many others throughout the country.
It was a beautiful idea expressed in a general way in these words, that no one should be any worse off for having participated in the war and no one should be any better off for not having participated in the war. I believe that we should strive earnestly toward that ideal, and I wish the minister to understand that he will have my complete support in every effort he makes to give the widows of our veterans of the first war a better deal, so that they will be able to pass the remaining years of their lives in something like comfort.

In connection with this item which has to do with pensions for the Riel rebellion veterans of 1885, I should like to know how many of the volunteers who participated in that rebellion are receiving pensions today, and also whether consideration has been given to extending these pension privileges to volunteers who served in the rebellion but were not attached to any units? I mention in that connection the case I brought to the attention of the house the other day. In Prince Albert and also in the area immediately west of Rosthern and the Duck Lake area there are a number of old men today-because, after all, sixty-three years have gone by since that rebellion-who took part in that rebellion, who maintained law and order during that rebellion, who suffered in consequence of their loyalty to the crown, but, because they were not attached to regular units are not permitted to receive any pension allowance. The other day I mentioned Mr. Angus McKay of the city of Prince Albert, a man of eighty-nine years of age, who finds himself in extreme financial difficulties. There are others in the same position. The old guard is practically gone today. There are a few left. If the minister can do anything toward relieving their situation by having them included under this head I know he would. No great expense would be entailed by his department and a great deal of good would be done.
If the minister and the committee would allow me, because I was called out of the house, I should like to refer to one other matter as well. It does not come under this head. I ask the indulgence of the committee. It has to do with the imperial South African veterans who, following the Boer war, as a result of advertising inducing them to come
Supply-Veterans Affairs

to this country, came here and established themselves. I ask that consideration be given to them so that they can qualify for veterans allowances. I am not going into a great many details in connection with the South African veterans who served in the imperial army, but I wish to quote a letter that appeared recently in the Regina Leader, which was written by Mr. M. C. Brown of Disley, in which is summarized the whole argument on behalf of these veterans. In part, he says this:	.
If we could turn the calendar back to September, 1902, we would find Aldershot, England, cluttered up with Canadian literature, asking all discharged South African vets to come to Canada and make new homes and share in this wonderful heritage. We were told there were opportunities out here and were led to believe we would receive the same treatment as their own South African veterans. When we also recollect that Great Britain paid all Canada's expenses in this war, even to the men's pay, surely they could assume a little responsibility for our welfare out here.
Then he goes on to say:
In 1930 the government introduced the old Veterans' Allowance Act. We were kept out again after being Canadian citizens for twenty-eight years. Whilst their own South African veterans have been provided with a pension in case of sickness, the imperial veteran has been relegated to relief. Our veteran societies have been trying for years to get us included in the Veterans' Allowance Act but without success.
I have also a letter from Mr. John. Nicks of Grand Coulee, Saskatchewan, president of the South African Veterans' Association, bringing the matter to my attention and, no doubt, to the attention of the minister. When the minister replies I would appreciate his dealing with the latter question as well. I want to thank the committee and you, Mr. Chairman, for giving me the opportunity of bringing these two matters to the attention of the minister although strictly speaking one of them is not before the committee at the moment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Three. Two veterans and one dependent.
S15.000 a year for these?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
This takes in other things besides that. It provides for disability of veterans of the Northwest rebellion, and disability incurred by members of the active militia during service prior to August 4, 1914, and compensation for death or injury resulting

from a fight undertaken in the course of duty in the public service and for a person employed in the public service or employed under the direction of any department of the public service of Canada. This vote is for these three objects, but there are two Riel rebellion veterans and one dependent.

Surely if there are just these few people the plea for an increase should be granted. I know one of these chaps very well; he is a fine old chap, cheerful and interested in national and international affairs. He is a splendid citizen. He was somewhat shocked a few years ago, on the institution of these pensions, to find that when he got his pension his old age pension was cut off because, under the federal regulations, he could not be receiving the two amounts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member is speaking of the war veteran's allowance. This is a disability pension.

I do not see any vote in reference to the South African veterans. Supply-Veterans Affairs

speechtext: If he was domiciled in Canada before he volunteered for service.
He was born here.

The veteran is entitled to war veterans' allowance?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes; I think there are four hundred of them receiving allowances.

I should like to bring up a matter which does not come under this item, and I have waited all afternoon to ask the question. Instead of bringing it up again, I should like to ask the question now. What is the attitude of the government with regard to the imperial veterans of the Boer war who came to Canada in 1902, 1903 and 1904 as a result of advertising that they were to be treated as Canadians who served in South Africa? Has consideration been given to allowing them the war veterans' allowance? If so, what is the present position?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The position is the same as in regard to anyone not domiciled in Canada before he went to fight in either the Canadian or the British forces or the allied forces. He must have been domiciled in Canada before he can qualify for the benefits. Those who came from South Africa afterwards are not qualified for these benefits.
Does the government intend to consider an extension to them?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot speak for the government-
You are the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -but what I envision and I hope will be accomplished some day- the Minister of Finance is not close, to me- is that, first of all, we shall get war veterans allowances for all Canadians who served here or in England or in a theatre of war, and that will justify us in considering the cases my -hon. friends mention, imperials and South Africans who came here afterwards in 1903 and 1904.

figures that were given earlier this evening by the minister, the number of pensioners bf tlhe first world wrar was, Canadians, 87,318, and the second world war, Canadians 87,558, and it is only a little more than 200 more for the second world war as compared- with the first. There are times for herring, and there are times when all the fish come together. There w'ere times when pensions were -awarded to anyone, even to -those not deserving, and afterwards there were times when the deserving ones could not get anything. Therefore I insist again on a check-up. I find, after thirty years, -the number of -Canadians who received pensions for world war I, 87,318, is quite -high, and the British in Canada, 250, and allied, 34, according to the figures. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Soldier Settlement and Veterans Land Actlt7)t. To provide for the cost of administration of soldier settlement; British family settlement; general land settlement, and Veterans Land -Act including engineering and other investigational planning and subdivision expenses that do not add tangible value to real property, $6,747,046.

This brings us to the subject of the soldier settlement and Veterans Land Act administration. This afternoon the minister, in referring to the settlement of soldiers on the land, used this expression: ' The larger operation has been tremendously
Supply-Veterans Affairs

successful." I must remark that that observation would not have any application to the administration of the Veterans' Land Act, or the minister has not perused the evidence taken recently before the public accounts committee concerning the administration of that act. I must be brief. To do the subject justice would require much more time than is now available. All I propose to do, therefore, is to review, as briefly as I can, some significant features in the investigation recently made on behalf of the house by its public accounts committee.
The Veterans' Land Act scheme contemplated the construction of about 2,600 units, 2,381 of which are completed in a sense. They are completed in the sense that the contractor, we are told, has left the work. The particular inquiry of the public accounts committee centred around the project at Sarnia, but I wish to make it abundantly clear to this committee of supply that that is not a peculiar situation at Sarnia. We had the evidence of Mr. Murchison, director of the Veterans' Land Act, that it was one of the worst, but he gave a list of others which he put in this category, and those among the worst included the Braefoot project on Vancouver island, the Boucherville project in Quebec, and the project at Sackville, New Brunswick. We had evidence that there were many other projects where there were units which, though not as bad as those in the category I have mentioned, were nevertheless bad. The committee was invited to continue its inquiry by reviewing the conditions at Windsor, but in view of the imminence of prorogation and the desirability of submitting a report to the house the committee felt it could not go farther.
So far as I am concerned, as a member of the committee I have had a number of letters since from veterans settled in other projects. They have been reading in the papers about evidence taken before the public accounts committee, and they have indicated that they are prepared to tender parallel evidence with regard to the conditions in the projects on which they settled.
I summarize that part of my submission in this way. The evidence that was taken as to conditions at Sarnia, while that is a particularly bad project, is nevertheless evidence that can be duplicated to a degree in many other places in Canada.
In a word, the evidence that was submitted to the committee was shocking. There is no weaker word that will begin to do justice to the evidence brought before this committee. Again, it is difficult to be brief, and I know how precious time is at this stage.

These houses have cost Canada-there are eight of them in this project-$10,100 each. To give the committee an idea of the value of these houses, we had evidence that several builders had looked at them and said they could build the houses for $4,500 each. The plan was on a cost-plus fixed-fee basis. The contractor was from Windsor. These are small houses. The largest has six rooms. Each house is either a bungalow or one and a half stories. The figure I have given includes cost of necessary repairs undertaken within a matter of several months after the alleged completion of the houses and occupation by the veteran purchasers, and also the cost of remedial drainage work which is now in course of being carried out.
There was no drainage investigation before this work was commenced; even the most elementary precautions with regard to drainage were completely ignored. The project is located a mile and a half from lake Huron outside Sarnia, but there was not the slightest effort to ascertain the water-table.
Again, the figure I have mentioned does not include one cent of departmental overhead. That figure of $10,100 consists of outlay without any regard to overhead costs in this department of government.
The house construction is of about as bad a kind as one can possibly imagine. I am sure the evidence shocked even the most hardened members of the committee. I wish there were time to review it, but I am afraid there is not. The basement had water in it all last fall, all last winter and all last spring. There were two sump pumps in the basement pumping water out, because the level of the basement floor is much too low; and of course the cost of electricity for keeping the pumps in operation was borne by the veteran. There is a hole in the basement floor. Apparently the contractor had an idea that it would be necessary to operate the sump pump there indefinitely.' The evidence concerning all the other normal features of construction is just in keeping with that. I shall just read one or two extracts for the sake of brevity. Here is one at page 516. It is from the evidence of one of the veteran owners, Mr. Cleave, who gave evidence which, I think, had a profound effect on the committee, even though he had to submit to a good deal of badgering on the part of certain members. This is one extract at page 516 of the proceedings of the committee:
Q. Can you give us the nature of the repairs? A. Yes. For example the doors did not close. Another example, my bathroom sink started to come off the wall, so they took some plaster of paris and filled the crack in behind; and there were some cracks along the doorsills and they filled those with plaster of paris. There were

Supply-Veterans Affairs
big-headed nails driven into the hardwood flooring and they attempted to countersink them and in countersinking them split the flooring; and they puttied up cracks in the chimney. In one of the houses the kitchen cupboard has started to settle, it had settled about a half an inch or more so they moved the quarter-round-they didn't move it, they hit it with a hammer and knocked it down flush again.
Here is another extract at page 518;
Q. You were cataloguing a number of things that you said were wrong with the house at the time of the exchange of the correspondence in January. I do not think you had finished when there were some other questions. A. Well, the paint job and the plastering and the taping of the joints. I mentioned that. The windows have not been fitted properly into the sashes. They leaked rain in a bad wind storm. They told one of the fellows there they did not leak with storm windows on, but he said, "Am I supposed to leave storm windows on all summer?" That was one of the contractor's workmen who said that. As to my stairway they spray-painted the house inside. The stairway is boards which have been stained and varnished, but they neglected to clean off the spray spots before they varnished. Consequently I have a lot of light paint on the stairs. It looks just like the painters had moved out yesterday and did not get around to cleaning it up. It cannot be cleaned without being sanded.
Then there were the warped doors. There was plywood that was broken in one bedroom upstairs. The bathroom sink was coming off the wall. The floors were very badly done with big-headed nails showing through which naturally you cannot resand while they are showing through.

I have refrained up to this time from saying anything very nice about the minister, because I was afraid it might be taken as just one Scotch immigrant patting the back of another Scotch immigrant, but after what has been said by other hon. members, I make up for that omission now by saying that I appreciate what the hon. minister and the officers of his department have done in handling the cases which I have brought to their attention.
What I rise for now is to appeal again to the minister on behalf of the old soldier settlers. These old fellows are now reaching the eventide of their lives. Some of them owe as much on their farms today as they did when they gott them in 1920 or 1921. When they bought the farm wheat had a value of $2 and $2.50 a bushel. Then wheat dropped to $1, and 
still they have to pay for the farm bought on that old value of wheat. I have been through the same thing myself and I am talking from experience. I have bought cows for $150 and two or three years afterwards they they dropped to $25, and the same thing with horses. I could talk for an hour on this. But I appeal to the minister and his department to give further consideration to these old soldier settlers. They have lived under difficult conditions in the past twenty years, contending with drought, bad times, and many other things that beset a man in agriculture. They struggled on and r-aised their families, and during the last war they gave their sons, some of whom now lie in lands across the sea. Some of them came back and started in under the new settlement scheme. I am an old soldier myself, and I appeal to the minister in all sincerity to give these old soldiers further consideration. In' their youth they gave the best they had for Canada.
While I should like to join with the hon. member for Swift Current who said today that he was a good Canadian and was proud of what Canada had done for her returned men, I do not think that job will be complete until we do something for these old soldier settlers by wiping off that debt. I do not think there is a soldier in this land of Canada who would object to wiping off that debt and giving these old soldiers a clean sheet in the eventide of their lives.

speechtext:
I should like to say a few words in reply to what the hon. member for Eglinton has said in regard to the Veterans' Land Act. At this Late hour I regret that he made the violent attack he did on the administration and on this whole housing project. I do not want to detain the committee unduly, but there were some things he said which perhaps should be replied to.
First, in regard to the cost of these houses, it is quite true that when all the drainage is done and the repairs are made and the houses are fully fixed up, the cost will average $10,100 each. Sarnia was admittedly the worst experience encountered in regard to these houses. The inspector in charge was a qualified architect, appointed through the ordinary processes of the civil service commission, but he did not keep a firm hand on the project and he is no longer with the department.
In regard to auditing, the auditing has been under the constant supervision of the cost and audit division of the treasury department, which has been in charge of disbursements from the very outset.
In regard to the suggestion of the appointment of a royal commission, the hon. member

made a great deal of the fact that the committee apparently were somewhat sympathetic; he seemed to think they went along with him in his criticism, at least to some extent. It seems to me that in his demand for a royal commission there is quite a bit of dramatics.
Far from it.
I asked for a royal commission in the committee, but they did not go the whole way with me. The report before the house is a majority report. The committee came part of the way but not far enough.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon. member had such faith in the committee he should have been satisfied with their recommendations, but apparently he wanted to go farther.
In regard to the committee which travelled across Canada and looked into these housing projects, it seemed to me that the hon. member w'as suggesting that their report copld not be relied upon. I do not think there is a member of this house apart from the hon. member for Eglinton who would suggest that a report which was made by the respected deputy minister of this department would not be absolutely reliable and in the best interests of the veteran. I think the hon. member will probably stand alone in criticizing the most respected returned soldier in Canada, who now occupies the position of deputy minister. He had joined with him in that work of the committee the director of the Veterans' Land Act. Perhaps he might not be regarded as entirely impartial by my hon. friend because he was inspecting work which had been done under his department. But in addition there was Colonel Parrish, director of housing for the Canadian Legion, and an expert on housing. Surely he could be relied upon to make an impartial report.
The hon. member for Eglinton suggested that these houses could be built for $4,500. When he went .that far I think the committee could pretty well decide how much attention to pay to the rest of his remarks. Actually the committee had before it evidence ^ to the cost of similar houses in other parts of Canada where admittedly very good work was done. For example, take Kamloops. The houses which in Sarnia, without taking into account the cost of repairs and so on, cost
$9,080 to build, cost $7,674 in Kamloops. The cost in Edmonton, where admittedly some of the most efficient building was done, was $7,143 for a similar house. Therefore, when the hon. member says that nothing has been done I do not understand why he makes that statement. He suggests that nothing has been done for the veteran to write down the cost of these houses. I do not understand why he makes that statement. It makes me wonder whether he knows anything about this matter.
The committee had before them a statement showing the make-up of .the sale price of these houses, and they used this formula. They found that the cost of these houses was fifty-eight cents a cubic foot. They found that the average cost throughout Canada was forty-four cents. To make sure that 'the veterans in these cases got a fair deal, they wrote down .the cost of these houses to forty cents a cubic foot or four cents under the average. That was done by the deputy minister under the order in council and the director of the Veterans' Land Act.
Before the houses were completed or these repairs became necessary. Since then there has not been a cent taken off.
