He made lots of statements with which I did not agree and which I thought were wrong, but I thought I would wait and try to put the facts before the committee as quickly, shortly and concisely as I could. Goodness knows I do not want to get into an argument or a brawl with the hon. member at this late hour. I am putting the facts before the committee as best I can.
In regard to the cost of these houses to the veterans, I have a statement here. When the cost was written down, as I have said, the actual amounts payable by the veterans ran from $6,047, $6,359, $6,504, $6,056, $6,324, $6,324, to $5,493. From all of this there was the statutory conditional grant of $1,400, leaving the amount that these veterans had to pay, after making their initial payment of $600, a monthly payment of $27.11, $24.34, $28.66, $24.34, $29.39. $27.15, $28.48 and $28.48. Hon. members will see that the highest amount that the veterans had to pay for these houses was $29.39, and that the lowest was $24.34. That is not rental. When the veteran pays that over a period of twenty-five years he is the owner of the house. Comparable rents for houses like these at that time would range from $45 to $50 at the very minimum. These payments are actually far under the average rentals at that time. Therefore, when it is said by the hon. member that the veteran has not been protected in this matter; that somehow he is being mistreated, when you have these payments which will count double for the veteran as against rentals being charged under different schemes of from $45 to $50 a month, I do not understand the hon. member's attitude.
As I say, I do not want to start a controversy at this time. I am trying to give the facts to the committee as best I can. In regard to the veterans in this proposition, the price was reduced in the way I have said to a fair comparison with houses in the same district. That is the first thing. Then the veteran was allowed to go into occupation without signing any contract, and he has been in occupation since late last year. He paid his $600 down and has paid no rent other than that $600 initial payment. Some of them have been in occupation since last October and have paid no rent at all. In addition to that, all the defects which have been pointed out are being remedied at no cost whatever to the veteran, so that the veteran is getting a house that is fully fixed up, that is brought down to the average cost of 40 cents a cubic foot, which is at least equal to, if not under, the average cost of all houses around there. He will have

his $1,400 conditional writeoff to which he is entitled under the Veterans' Land Act and, of course, when he signs his contract he gets all of the rights I have just mentioned.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I shall deal with one or two other items that the hon. member mentioned. Colonel Parrish mentioned, for example, that the average cost for the whole of Canada of houses like these was $7,150. He found that to be reasonable in today's market, and that is his opinion. Of course everybody in the committee will have no difficulty in accepting Colonel Parrish's opinion against that of the hon. member for Eglinton.
In regard to the cost being excessive, these houses were constructed by the Department of Veterans Affairs in an endeavour to make a contribution to the housing situation. It was known there would be a great shortage, and so the Veterans' Land Act administrator jumped into this picture and did his little bit. It is quite true that perhaps in the light of what we know now, if he had been another type of public servant who said, "I will not do any more than I absolutely have to; I will not stick my neck out; I will be very careful," he would not be under this attack today ; but instead of that, being a returned soldier himself who served overseas in the first war, and having some real anxiety to help returned soldiers in the second world war, he thought he could make a little contribution in having his organization build some houses on these small holdings. It was the request of a committee of the house that he should do this. As the result of his action, over 2.000 people own nice little houses across this country. I visited a lot of them. I have talked to the people in them and I have seen how happy they were. There has been a great attempt to decry these houses. I have been in them in various parts of this country. Wherever I have gone and talked to the women and the men. in the houses, I found they were delighted to be able to have a nice little, home to go into on terms as reasonable as these were. Therefore I say-in spite of the break-down here and there, which is not the responsibility of the administrator, because, after all, public servants are hired by the commission; all that can be done when they break down is to dismiss them, to let them go, and that has been done in these cases-what we have today is a situation where the department went into a housing activity to try to help out the returned soldier to establish himself, with a staff provided by the civil service commission which has broken down here and there. They have worked under terrible difficulties. Anybody today who has tried to build a house knows the

Supply-Veterans Affairs
difficulty. For example, they could not get glass, which meant that the houses could not be closed in. Then moisture entered into the houses and we had swelling of the lumber and the floors in the houses and continued trouble. If you could not get the material you needed and you had to let your labouring men go then, of course, you could not get them 'when you did get the material. These things all ran up the cost. Anybody who has tried to do any building in the last couple of years knows the difficulty that anyone was under in that regard.
It is very easy to come along now and criticize. We know of these great difficulties. There were break-downs here and there. It is very easy to come along and make a passionate appeal to the house, make out that the public servants, public-spirited servants are, in some way, deserving of censure. But I ask the committee to put themselves in the position of the director of the Veterans' Land Act, to consider his motives in trying to help out, consider the difficulties he was up against and realize that he could not personally supervise these numerous enterprises from one end of Canada to the other; that he had to rely on people who were picked-there was a shortage of skilled people-to do this work. There was a great expansion of work. Those that have broken down have been released. There has been no attempt at any time to conceal anything. There has been a complete disclosure in this house, the fullest possible disclosure. It seems to me that an attempt to make a great deal of a thing like this is really an attempt to take advantage of a situation which is, of course, pretty well prevalent all over Canada with anyone who is trying to build.
As regards this excessive feature, it was realized that- costs were becoming excessive owing to uncontrollable factors, and the government, on its own initiative, provided this million right off, put on an inspection by the deputy minister and these other gentlemen, and made sure that the veterans would not suffer by the steps taken.
On the question as to whether contractor liability is being investigated, what more can be done? Wherever it was considered that anything was wrong it was turned' over to the mounted police and the -assistance of the Department of Justice was enlisted, so that if there was a possibility of making the contractor liable it would be established. That was done a long time ago without any demand for it by any member of parliament.

Does the hon. gentleman
say that the Department of Justice was consulted1?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Before it ever came to this house.
That is not what was brought out in the committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it was. Anyway, that is the fact I am. giving to the committee. These veterans wanted homes over their heads. It was not known what it would cost to fix these places up; they were told they could move in if they made a S600 payment, and when the time came to fix the cost they could sign a contract or, if they did not wish to do so, there was no compulsion on them to buy. I have a long list of persons who are anxious to get into houses. For every man able to get in-, there are -ten who w-ould be glad to.
That is not true of Sarnia.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I know it is so in most cases. A real contribution has been made in providing 2,300 homes. The director frankly admitted that the department had been poorly served by certain subordinate officials and that was seized upon as the basis of an attack. Because he was frank and honest to admit that some of his officials had not served the department as well as they should have done- their connection with the department having been terminated in consequence-he is attacked. But what more could be done? It was undoubtedly for the civil service commission to obtain the necessary number of competent inspectors, superintendents and so on, experienced in the work. The civil service commission did the best they could. Every member of this house believes that the right way to go about -the matter is to have the civil service commission do it, and if they are to do it, then it is to be expected that they will do the best they can.
The chief engineer of the Veterans' Land Act administration and 20 other officials in the branch have been permitted to resign or have been released from the department. In other words, there has been no sparing of those who have not done a good job so far as this work is concerned.
I 'have tried to run over these things as quickly as I can because I know -that the house is anxious to get through, and- I have tried my best to give some of the highlights in this matter.
Has the hon. gentleman read the evidence taken before the public accounts committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, I have.
Have you read it all?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I have not read the last page of it but most of it.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
Most of it has not yet been printed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I have it in typewritten form.
Did the hon. gentleman read the evidence of the director of the Veterans Land Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did.
And all the exhibits?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I will not say I read every page.
I thought not, judging by some of the remarks the hon. member made, because they do not jibe with the evidence given before the committee by the director of the Veterans Land Act.

I suppose this matter will be threshed out later. I do not wish to deal with the situation in Sarnia, about which I know nothing. But there is one matter which the hon. member for Selkirk spoke of and in regard to which many hon. members have continued to ask for information over a period of years, and that is special consideration for the few noble veterans of the last war, who, under the soldier settlement board, are trying to carry on. After having lived with some of these veterans, having witnessed their efforts, having seen thousands of them finally give up in despair because they could not carry on, their homes broken, the result of years of toil, years of difficulty, having disappeared, I submit that something should be done for these people. I do not know whether it wras the minister or the deputy minister who was responsible for the policy of the department and the consequent absolute failure of the board with respect to thousands of soldiers who tried to settle on the land and who apparently have failed to impress the department with the hopelessness of their situation. A plea has been made in this house for a number of years that special consideration be. given these few men who are now struggling, in the declining years of their lives, to carry on with a debt over their heads. Last year the officials tried to tell us that these soldiers were now in a position to pay up and that everything would be satisfactory for them. I should like to know how many have been able to pay the balance of their indebtedness during the past year, how many have quit or have signed a quit-claim deed, either voluntarily or under pressure, and how many of these soldiers are still left in the various provinces trying to struggle on and to pay off the balance even in their declining years.

One other thing. What decision has been arrived at by the government with regard to these men in the future? Are more of these men to be deprived of their homes because they cannot pay up, or has the department come to a decision? The director of the Veterans' Land Act has been given complete control. The decision is entirely his. He is granted a seal and the contract is put in his name. He is czar of the situation from end to end. I want to know what the situation is at the present time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
In the five-year period ended March 31, 1947, there were 3,408 settlers who repaid loans in full and received title.
Mr. CA'STLEDEN: Have you the figures for the last year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I will see if I can get them. There are 250 who have assigned their contracts to other purchasers, and have taken equities in cash. Soldier settlers during that period paid in cash on contracts $6,441,335. Ninety per cent of all soldier settlers made payment on their contracts in the five-year period, and the record of payment of taxes is equally good. There are 3,453 settlers left, and I am advised that they are generally in a good position. It is estimated that eighty-five per cent wdll have little difficulty paying off loans under the present contracts. The average age is fifty-seven, and it is, of course, recognized that there are some difficult cases. Where there is a case of advancing years or recurring disabilities or serious family illnesses, these cases will continue to receive individual and sympathetic attention. Any suggestion that soldiers have been thrown off these lands is, I am advised, absolutely untrue.
I have seen soldiers thrown off.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am told that during this five-year period no one has been thrown off.
Or asked to sign a quitclaim deed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: In a few cases they have voluntarily turned the contract over to somebody else; but I am told that nobody has been thrown off against his will.
Nobody has been compelled to sign a quit-claim deed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs

speechtext: It is a new experience for me to be getting into this sort of argument. I have been content to represent Renfrew North without endeavouring to be a statesman. I have no ambitions along that line. I am thankful to say that in Renfrew North, as far as I know, we have nothing but satisfaction with the work of Mr. Murchison. My experience with Mr. Murchison as a government official is limited. I met him a number of times in his office in connection with his work of buying land for the purpose of settling veterans on farms; and in my opinion a splendid job was done in any case that I know of, particularly from the veteran's angle. I thought Mr. Murchison was always rather miserable about the price he wanted to pay for the farms. He might have paid more money, and would have been perfectly justified in paying a good deal more money in some cases. As an official looking after the settling of veterans on farms, I think he did a splendid job. I have not been in the habit of mixing up actively in the proceedings of any committee of which I was a member, but I did mix up in this public accounts committee on this particular question, largely because the hon. member for Eglinton kept Mr. Murchison on the mat for six hours a day, standing on his feet, and being treated as a common criminal. The hon. member for Eglinton is the type of lawyer who, when he gets his knife into a man, is not satisfied with that but must keep on twisting it.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Police court stuff.

I did work up enough sympathy to interest myself rather actively in this housing project up in Sarnia township. We heard the whole story about these houses
from the hon. member for Lambton West, and I was not greatly impressed with the awful defects of those houses. Those houses had been built in the winter time. I know something about the difficulty of getting lumber, because I live in a wood country.- Lumber buyers would come from Sarnia or any other district, with ten-ton trucks, if they could get a load of green lumber from any little sawmill. We could sell anything. A man could go into his swamp and cut down poplar or balm of Gilead which could ordinarily be sold only for pulpwood prior to the war. But these lumber buyers would grab up that material as good building lumber. What happens when you get that kind of lumber? Everyone knows. It must be remembered that it was green. Not a board of dry lumber could be bought. Some of our best operators of factories in Renfrew North would' fairly weep about putting this green lumber right from the mill through a planer, knowing that it would go into a building. What will happen in a case of that kind? Everybody knows. The concrete is run in the winter time.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member
knows what he is talking about.
He does not know what he is talking about.

The hon. member the other day talked about kiln-drying the lumber. That was silly enough, and I think shows how much he knows about it. It is silly to talk about kiln-drying lumber for all the housing construction which is going on all across this country. One per cent of it could not be kiln-dried.
The specifications did not call for green lumber.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.

No, they did not; that is true. I do not know this contractor, and I am not apologizing for the work which was done there. He probably did not do a perfect job. I do not hold any brief for that contractor, but I can easily understand how a contractor could take on the job of building eight houses in that particular district, having in mind being able to buy dry pine or spruce. There was difficulty on account of the labour situation and lack of material. A priority had to be obtained for nails. I have known times when not a farmer in the country could buy nails in any hardware store in Renfrew county. There were plenty of times when that situation prevailed. I can see how a contractor would come in and find a different
Supply-Veterans Affairs

set-up from that which he had expected. Instead of getting the lumber he wanted at the time he wanted it, he would have to drive all over the country and then in many cases would have to accept this inferior green lumber. He could lose his shirt overnight at that kind of thing; and probably did for all I know. I do not know whether or not he made a dollar, but his case will be heard in court-
As long as he did not lose his pants, he will be all right.

-and that ought to satisfy even the hon. member for Eglinton. Just out of idle curiosity, during the last two or three years I have been watching a couple of projects around here. I like driving out around the experimental farm. Out the Merivale road there is a 400-family project. Then out beyond Boggs' there is another one. I think that is on what is called the Prescott highway. Two years ago this summer, the contractors were working on those projects, and it just looked like a bog hole. I saw them last fall, and they still looked like bog holes. I saw them recently, and this Merivale project is now getting around to the place where the finishing touches are being put on. Driveways are being put in. It is just a splendid, lovely community. Any person at all would be proud to own one of those houses. There is one thing we must keep in mind. Not one of these veterans is paying anything more than a modest rent, and in a period of years -twenty-five, I believe-he will own the house. The veterans pay a modest rent of anywhere from S20 to perhaps as high as $30 a month in some cases. It is a most interesting suggestion which comes from the hon. member for Eglinton who would appoint a royal commission to go around this country investigating this housing situation just because those eight houses may not have been perfect. Under the circumstances, some defects were sure to develop. Those houses could not have been so very bad. This young man Cleave who was here as a witness, who never went overseas, went and investigated the house himself. He looked it over and was satified with it. Nothing more might have come of the matter if the hon. member for Lambton West had not happened along and seen the odd crack in the wall or noticed a draught coming under a door, which is just about all these defects amount to when you come to look them over. There is a long list, of course; but in the committee I made this remark-and I think I was quite safe-that I could get two men from Renfrew county who would go into any of these houses and complete all the repairs you are talking about inside a week.
Then do you censure the government for spending $6,000 on these repairs now?

If I were censuring anybody it would be the hon. member for Eglinton for making so much noise about something I do not think is worthy of it.
Here is how I regard the suggestion of appointing a royal commission. We have communists in this country; and what is the communist way of working? It is to get out and encourage discontent. If there is no discontent they go out and create it. That is the communist idea, and to me it looks as though this were just a nice communist method of creating discontent among satisfied veterans. I should like to be on that commission. It would be a grand way to spend a couple of years seeing Canada from coast to coast at the expense of the taxpayers. So I say to the minister that if he appoints a royal commission I want to be on it. We could start right here in this lovely community on the Merivale road, provided that we had an advance agent; and I think the hon. member ter Lambton West would make a fine advance agent. Give him a start of a week or two; he could create a great deal of discontent in that lovely community. It is quite. easy to do; go in and take a look around and say, "There is a crack in the wall of this house, and that is not fair. That crack should not be there." The first thing you knew you would have a regular hornets' nest. We could spend a couple of months right here investigating that sort of thing. They say the climate on the west coast is a little better, so that we could leave that for the winter time.
And the houses are worse.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not in Kamloops.
Yes, they are.
That is right; you could spend a few months there.

I have tried to look at 'this matter in a broad way. Do not think for a moment I was ever fond of the idea that the government should be forced into the construction of houses. I did not like the idea, and I was never anxious that any of my veterans should take on a project of this kind. I do noit like the instalment plan. If I buy a house I want to pay for it and own it. I am the pioneer type. If I am going to build a house I want to have a woodlot where I can cut the logs, saw them up and leave them for a year until the lumber is dry; and

Supply-Veterans Affairs
then do a good deal of tihe work myself. My wife and I started in last fall to build a house, and I am sure labour is not as difficult to obtain where I live as it is around the Windsor area. We started in and I found myself driving the horses on the scraper. Then it became hard to get labour and I found myself doing the whole job alone, not only driving the horses but guiding the scraper. However, we got that pant done; we got a roof over the house, and we hope to complete that bouse soon. We have had to wait plenty for material, and I certainly have a great deal of sympathy for any contractor who undertook to build a block of houses, with the difficulties he must face in regard to labour, lack of materials, and all the rest- of it.
The hon. member for Eglinton has certainly twisted the knife in poor Murchison's back tonight, and I do not think it was deserved. He was doing his job as well as he could, but he was encumbered with a great many duties. That man had so much work to do he should never have had to go outside his office.

If the hon. member
would permit a question, in the committee did he vote for this report when it came up for adoption?

That report did not
satisfy me. I did not care for it.

Did the hon. member
vote for it?
There was not a vote.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I
am telling the hon. member he voted for this report, in which there is this sentence:
Your committee was not favourably impressed by the way evidence was given by Mr. Gordon Murchison . . .
Perhaps the hon. member will say why he turned the knife in Mr. Murchison's back in ithat report.

I did my best to have
that sentence taken out, because I did nor think it was a fair expression. That sentence should not be in the report.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member for Humboldt, who would have the floor, would allow the hon. member for Peterborough West to speak, since he wishes to catch a train at eleven o'clock.

I have something to say
along the line of what has been said by *the hon. member for Eglinton, but the hon. member for Peterborough West might go ahead.

I shall be very brief. I want to ask a few questions regarding the houses at Stratford1. I understand 'that eight houses were built there in 1945, but that the sewers for those houses are below the level of the Stratford sewers and, as a consequence, those houses have neveT been occupied. I understand, further, that the department have pumps in the houses trying bo keep them dry. Evidently they were built in what might be described as a sunken garden, similar to the oase in Sarnia. Is that the fact?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
We are still awaiting installation andi connection with the city sewer.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

But since the sewers are so much below the level of the city sewers, it is doubtful if you will ever be able to connect up with them, and you have pumps in there now. For two years the veterans have been waiting to get into these houses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Negotiations are going on with the city to have these houses connected with the city sewer. Apparently it is possible to have that done; it is just a matter of coming to an agreement with the city.
Are you gradually training the water to run uphill?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: There are, I am told, ways of raising water without having it run uphill.

During the speech of the hon. member for Eglinton, the minister said the Tories were trying to keep the boys out of their houses for a year. This is a case of keeping them out for two years and perhaps more. I could say a great deal more on this matter, but I am not going to do so. I understand that a watchman has been maintained there for over a year, who is paid so much a month by the department, until such time as these sewers are connected. How long will it be before the sewers will be connected?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Apparently it will be three or four months before the veterans can be permitted to go into the houses; that is, before the houses will be finished to the point where they can be occupied. Obviously there has to be someone to watch the houses until they oan be inhabited, and that will not be charged up against the veteran when he signs the contract.

This place, so far as water is concerned, is as bad as if not worse than the Sarnia situation, where there has to be drainage out to the township line, and no contract has been made with the township to take the water away from this project involving forty-three houses. The drainage system in Sarnia has not yet been connected with the township. That will cause a delay in the Sarnia scheme.

At this late hour I have no desire to go into detail on the points raised by the hon. member for Eglinton, and the further discussion entered into by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, and some other members on the Liberal side. However, having been a member of the public accounts committee, and as one
[Mr. Tucker.)
from the C.C.F. group, I did consider it necessary to say a few words on this all-important question.
When the Minister of Veterans Affairs was asking permission to have the house sit a little longer tonight, I had intended saying to him that if he would just let me say my piece we might get through with the rest of his estimates.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs has something on his hands that he cannot explain just by a wave of the hand, and there are a few things I would draw to the attention of the committee. The hon. member dealt with the cost per house at Sarnia, and the average for Canada. While it is correct that the Sarnia cost was fifty-eight cents per cubic foot and the average for Canada was about forty-four cents per cubic foot, it must be remembered that not only has the Sarnia project fallen below the requirements laid down by the contract signed by the department and the contractors, but there are other projects which have cost more money than they should have and which do not contain the workmanship they should have, in view of the money spent on them. The result is that the average cost for Canada as a whole has been raised.
I do not wish to go into detail at this time of night. However, having sat in the committee and having heard every bit of evidence given when this matter was under consideration, I must say I was amazed to see that things of that kind could be allowed to go on without having more drastic action taken by the department than has been taken.
We are now at the stage where the committee has reported. While I admit frankly that that report is not as strong in some respects as some of us would have liked to see it,, on the other hand it is more or less of a compromise, as of necessity are all reports from parliamentary committees, if they are going to report at ail.
That report does fairly generally reflect the consensus of the great majority of members who served on the committee. I should like to take this opportunity to compliment most members of that committee who took such great pains to be in attendance at the meetings and who took such an active interest in the hearings. I would compliment the chairman and all those who made it possible to carry on the work of the committee with the sole idea of seeing, first, that the veterans receive value for their money and, secondly, that the taxpayers of this country shall not be called upon to pay exorbitant costs for the construction of these houses.

Inquiries oj the Ministry
My suggestion to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, to his parliamentary assistant and to the government is that the report tabled in the house the other day is the result of painstaking work by a standing committee of the house. I would urge upon t'he government and all its supporters that they read that report carefully, and especially would I urge the minister and the government to endeavour to see that the report is acted upon. After the committee has given its time and attention to this work, I do not think that at this time, in the dying hours of the session, we can thresh out this matter to the satisfaction of anyone. While the hon. member for Eglinton may not have got his royal commission, which he and some of the rest of us might have been inclined to favour, nevertheless the report does make a suggestion to the government. I say that if the government fails to act upon that report and to see that justice is done, and if it fails to see that the veterans get value for their money, and that the taxpayers get value for the money they must spend, then the government must be held accountable in the future. For the time being, however, I am prepared to let the government have an opportunity to act upon that report.
Eleven o'clock.
